Sr. A. Maria Eletta Convertini

ROSA GATTORNO, A MOTHER

English text of Rosa Gattorno, una madre (Rome 1987); the quotations of Mother Rosa are taken from her original texts

Preface by Fr. Valentino G. Macca di S. Maria, OCD

Mother Rosa: what richness of spirit and of humanity!

Humble and recollected, wrapped in a mystery of simplicity and nobility, always with her gaze turned to God, her Love, and with eyes attentive to all, especially to the humble and the most forgotten. She is a mystic and at the same time a woman of great, tireless activity, with two eyes that penetrated deep into the soul of those who met her. To meet her once was enough to keep her memory as a continual presence; a presence through which one felt drawn near to God. She made people feel well and serene, reconciled them with their own lives, led them to love life more even in the time of the cross and of suffering; she was a stimulus to pray more and to smile, to open the heart and the purse more to the poor, to the last; she drew others to become like her: a gift of gentle, attentive and effective charity for anyone in need of a smile, a word of encouragement and help. Above all it was like experiencing what God had communicated to her with so much strength and abundance when he had molded her with so rich and sensitive a spirit of a Mother. All those who could know her intimacy in a special way, and not only her Daughters, had the sensation of finding in her a wonderful and visible reflection of the tenderness of God, who for each of us is more than a Mother, as St. Thérèse of Lisieux said, basing herself on Scripture.

It was the joyful experience of her contemporary witnesses, who recounted it with emotion: an ever living and sweet memory of her maternal face when she was at prayer and when she was at the service of the poor; when she opened herself to that communion so supernatural and so human that in God one sensed her, more than a sister, as a Mother ready to give life mysteriously. Was it not he who called her to be Mother, now and forever?

A study of her personality that reveals this maternal aspect of Rosa Gattorno is therefore to be welcomed with joy. It is a gift that helps one, in prayer and contemplation, to penetrate that particular maternal gift which is Rosa.

In his Providence God arranged that at the age of twenty-two Rosa should marry Gerolamo Custo, becoming the mother of three children: Carlotta, Alessandro and Francesco. It was a sorrowful motherhood, even in the joy of the gift of self, because of the economic situation, the ruin of Gerolamo and, soon after, his illness and his death, still young, in March 1858. Rosa does not close in on herself: it is contrary to her nature. Alone, amid worries and anxieties, she opens herself more and more to the charism of motherhood toward her children and toward the poor, widening the richness of her heart and her love. More than before she is a Mother, and only a Mother! One might say that God plays with this young Genoese woman, drawing her to the center of his graces, deepening her motherhood and giving her a new face of chastity, to which she bound herself by vow after her husband’s death, adding soon after the vow of poverty: an interior richness for a greater gift of self, for which LOVE was preparing her.

It is in this perspective that, first in Genoa, she begins to experience a life oriented to religious consecration: a maternal initiative dedicated first to the Immaculate and then to St. Anne, at Piacenza and in Rome, in Via Merulana, where the Mother will spend her last years, to open herself to the light of the Redeemer in May 1900, when sister death would come to carry her soul into the bosom of him from whom all fatherhood takes its name, and all motherhood, as Pope John Paul I recalled in one of his catecheses.

Her program? To be a Mother.

Her name? Mother, and only Mother.

Her style? A motherhood that offers itself.

Her pedagogy? That of a Mother who cares, loves and serves.

As she wished to be a Mother, so she wanted her Daughters to be “little Mothers,” those called to positions of responsibility in the direction, formation and guidance of the Sisters. All this in the name of Mary and of the holy Mother St. Anne, whom the prophetic intuition of Fr. Bernardo M. Clausi of the Minims had indicated as the title of Mother Rosa’s Family.

The correspondence confirms the data of the Beatification and offers thousands of details on the spirit of Rosa Gattorno’s maternal formation. She was a woman of balanced personality who, without sentimentalism, sought strong women. She educated them with the grace that shapes through sacrifices, work, renunciation of self and total gift of self. She sought in each Daughter of St. Anne a Mother like herself, on the example of Anne and Mary, all intent on the gift of life, to God, in the Community and to brothers and sisters.

The publication of Mother Rosa’s correspondence reveals a treasure of tenderness and sweetness, her inner strength, a woman of delicate and noble intuition, attentive and respectful of different characters and gifts of nature and grace, firm in serving God’s plan for each person. But all the Letters, which are thousands upon thousands, reveal the Gift that God made to the Church in Rosa Gattorno, creating in her a heart so close to his own, totally committed to oblation, in a life joyfully determined to offer, nourish and perfect life in others.

The present study analyzes with sobriety and competence the gift of Mother Rosa Gattorno’s motherhood. These are not pious reflections or mere literary whims: it is serious research, founded on sure sources, on what can help to understand the Mother of the Daughters of St. Anne in the itinerary on which God guided her, first in her natural family, which blossomed from the sacrament that made her wife and mother on the natural and spiritual level, then in the Institute in which God willed to express her in fullness, if we may so dare to say.

It is the mystery of a motherhood simple and complex, tried and blessed, obstructed and rewarded beyond all expectation. It is not without surprise that one finds that in 1900, when Rosa concludes her earthly pilgrimage, her motherhood had extended even beyond the oceans. Almost 4,000 Sisters called her Mother and felt her to be such, although physically far from her, in the 368 communities in Italy, America and Africa: families where love reigns and each grows in the gift of love, under the sure guidance and the nearness of the heart of Mother Rosa.

In recent years work has resumed toward the conclusion of the Cause of Beatification. The study of the Processes, of the Mother’s Writings and of the vast and precious Documentation invites us to praise God for what he accomplished in his humble Servant. In all this gift of the Lord, in all her generous response to the Spirit of Jesus, one thing is evident: in Rosa the Father invites us to contemplate his love and his mercy, his goodness and his patience, his generosity, as they were welcomed and brought to perfection in the experience of the humble woman called to be at the origin of a religious experience of consecration under the name of the Mother of the Immaculate, St. Anne: a woman who will be a Mother forever. At the moment when Vatican II has called us back to the contemplation of the Church which, in Mary and with Mary, is Mother, is not the knowledge, the imitation and the invocation of Mother Rosa Gattorno a source of ecclesial hope?

This is the aim of the present work of Sr. A. Maria Eletta Convertini, the first, which invites many further inquiries and researches that may place in the soul the desire to know ever more this Mother whom God gave to the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne and to the whole Church. To find a Mother is to find the source of LIFE. That life which in Mother Rosa Gattorno was God, loved and served to the complete sacrifice for the joy of the children of God.

Valentino G. Macca di S. Maria, OCD

Postulator of the Cause of Mother Rosa

Rome, 25 March 1987

Solemnity of the Annunciation of the Lord

Who is Rosa Gattorno? She is a woman wonderfully rich in “gifts of nature and grace.” God entrusted to her a “special” mission of motherhood: to be at the service of life, in every condition and in a universal dimension, in the historical realities of her time. She expresses her generous and faithful response by offering God her whole life, in a relationship of mystical oblation and in apostolic action.

A “sign” of irrefutable evidence of her apostolic action is the development of the many communities of the religious “Family” founded by Mother Rosa in northern Italy and, with even greater success, in southern Italy, between 1866 and 1900. They were very “difficult” years for the Kingdom of Italy, only recently officially proclaimed, which had not yet overcome the troubled process of unification and the problems connected with it. Another sign of her apostolic action was the development of communities in South America and in Africa, in even more “difficult” circumstances. Another important sign was the fact that many young women entered among the Daughters of St. Anne, attracted by the charm of her charism, and called her “mother.”

These spiritual Daughters have handed on to future generations a faithful portrait, “narrating” and bearing witness to her life, developing veneration for her person and practicing in the concrete facts of each day what has historically preserved her memory, beginning with the collection of her writings, the publication of a first biography in 1937 and of a second in 1969, together with other studies on her personality. The second biography was published in order to make known to everyone that Mother Rosa is a person still relevant to the world of today. The number of lay people who are inspired by her witness as a strong and courageous woman is growing: they know that she belonged completely to God. Her motherhood is a gift welcomed not only by the Daughters of St. Anne, but also by a growing number of spiritual children. It is a sign of our time, which makes us attentive. Mother Rosa desires to express anew her mission of motherhood in today’s world, as difficult and full of problems as it was in her own time. How can this come about?

It is a question that many ask. Many people wish to know more about the life and work of Mother Rosa Gattorno; many try to listen to her voice, which almost “speaks” in her writings. The aim of this study is to offer an answer to the request to establish a historical “dialogue” with the Mother, and to the greater and deeper things that emerge from it: an answer founded on the examination of the original “sources,” consisting precisely of the very numerous Letters written by the Mother, of the letters of the Custo children and of the Daughters of St. Anne and, to a limited extent, of the Memoirs.

This study seeks to understand Mother Rosa in the perspective of motherhood, as a direct and personal subject in interpersonal relationships with her own children and with her spiritual children. It seeks to describe the richness of her maternal attitude, open to God and to persons, which is manifested to each one in the “climate” of feelings and attitudes, and to consider her action as inspired by the attitude of motherhood: this is the guiding thread of the research. The focus is exclusively on her, who writes and speaks, and who speaks to us through her writings. The quotations are therefore numerous. We regret that many have been deliberately omitted, for understandable editorial reasons, since the use of too many quotations would have been repetitive. All the material used in preparing the work is thus based not only on the quotations reported, but also on other similar ones not mentioned.

The sources, almost all still unpublished, lend authority to the present study. It is nevertheless only a limited approach to the correspondence and a limited contribution to the knowledge of Mother Rosa.

It is a very limited answer to the important questions concerning the life and work of Mother Rosa Gattorno, and a filial acknowledgment of gratitude toward Mother Rosa for her precious service to the Church and for her wonderful service to the cause of the Kingdom of God, which she served faithfully, giving “everything and even life.”

MOTHERHOOD:

THE HEART OF ROSA GATTORNO’S CHARISM

Awareness of the gift.

Motherhood is the heart of Rosa Gattorno’s vocational charism. Her whole person radiated the maternal feelings that flowed from her soul, and she was aware of being a messenger with the mission of conveying God’s love to others. For this reason she gave her “motherhood without limits and without reward.”1

Mother Rosa constantly devoted herself to forming the Daughters of St. Anne in the spirit of the family of the Holy Mother of Mary Immaculate.

She wrote to Sr. Francesca Camisa, the superior of the community of Sampierdarena:

“This poor mother of yours can do nothing else but raise prayers to the Lord every day, that he may make my daughter a great saint and give her the lights needed to direct her community well. Prudence, meekness and charity: with these three virtues, which I hope God the Father will grant me to give you, you will guide the Daughters of St. Anne, Mother of the Immaculate, on the way of perfection.”2

And to Sr. Adelaide Pezzoni:

“Charity, gentleness, the sweetness of the words of a mother who corrects her daughters, make it impossible for the sister’s heart not to correct itself and become a true Daughter of St. Anne.”3

Filled with maternal love, she treated the Sisters with gentleness and understanding. To Sr. Veneranda Picco, who complained about her silence, she wrote on 19 May 1879:

“My daughter … drive away all, all your sadness, and think that your mother holds you close every day in the heart of Jesus and that you are her pet (if one may say so). Ah! my little girl, when will you be persuaded of the affection I bear you? Farewell, yours, yours, for eternity.”

Her letters to her daughters contain and express, with unmistakable intensity, the treasure of tenderness and dedication of her motherhood, fully lived: she was a mother in the flesh, “by the will of man” (Jn 1:13), and she was a mother in the Spirit as well. She used to begin her letters with expressions of tender affection:

“My daughter,” “my beloved daughter,” “my daughter for all ages,” and other similar expressions, and she closed them with phrases such as: “your poor Mother”; “poor, but still your mother, believe me”; “I am your poor mother Rosa, now and for all eternity.”

It was dear to her that all the Daughters should call her by one name only: Mother. When Sr. Francesca Camisa, one of the first Sisters, thought it fitting to use the title “Foundress” in a letter to Mother Rosa, her reply, though couched in calm and affectionate language, was unusually severe:

“Francesca, my dear Superior, first of all, if you do not want me to send your letters back, change the address. Here is the address you must use: To Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno. If you do otherwise by even one word, I will send them back and will not write to you any more because, my dear, I have enough knives piercing me already, and this is for me a most repugnant word, that is, words that announce a purely infernal way. I never was anything and I am nothing. Out of your goodness you give me the name of Mother, although I do not deserve it.”4

She learned to be a mother by raising her children, Carlotta, Alessandro and Francesco: she carried them in her womb for nine months, saw them born and watched them grow.

She took care of them so that their lives might be beautiful and healthy.

She did the same with her spiritual Daughters, and she could not do otherwise. She explained this in a letter about two girls whom she had taken in as orphans in her community many years before and who wished to become Daughters of St. Anne:

“I am always your poor Mother, who holds you close in the heart of St. Anne, Mother of the Immaculate, and every day I recommend you to her and then I say to her: ‘Mother, look at these two dear little daughters of mine, who have grown up nourished by the milk of your providence, and I, poor me, had the good fortune to see them at my side when they were small, drinking in the holy teachings of our Catholic religion, becoming true Christians and one day brides of Jesus!’ What a consolation to think that I already have several such girls who are my adopted, legitimate, spiritual daughters, and one day will share eternal joy with me.”5

A mother, even when her children grow up and become mature and independent, keeps and strengthens the bonds of love with them. It is a law of motherly love, and Mother Rosa, like all mothers, obeyed this law. She wrote to Sr. Giuseppa Troni, who was in La Paz, Bolivia, on 21 May 1879:

“It is now already 20 days since I have heard from you, and I say: ‘What is my daughter Giuseppina doing? Perhaps she believes that those who have stayed behind do not feel the emptiness and the deprivation of being unable to see you?’ Oh, my daughters! Certainly those who are in Italy do not cost me so many prayers as you do. […] Ah! Be a little quicker in writing to me. And then I say: ‘Oh, what will they be doing?’ Since you have left me your heart and your will, I am faithful, and every day I offer it to God and press you to the heart of Jesus, and I pray to my dear Crucified One never to let you stray, and always to keep you within Himself. Oh, sweet dwelling, where nothing else is found but love and joy! You who desire to find joy, hold yourselves close to Him, and in Him you will find love and joy — a love that gives every kind of sweetness! I hope you will tell me many things, for I long for it so much. Farewell, and remember that I am your mother; it is true that I am poor and ugly, but still I will repeat to you: ‘I am your mother!’ Even poor children, even if their mother is ugly and poor, still love her, because she is their mother, and they prefer her to a princess or a noblewoman of the earth. Enough. I want to banish from my mind the wicked thought that so afflicts me, that you might have forgotten me or that your hearts might not be attached to me!!! No, no! I see that these are sad thoughts, and I want to banish them.”6

Apart from the force and emphasis of her style (almost hammering in the insistence of its imperatives, such as “think,” and in the repeated “I am your mother”; note also the “but still”), these last sentences seem to express in synthesis the clear awareness of motherhood that Mother Rosa lived. In her life, motherhood is a reality experienced first as motherhood in the flesh, through the will of man, and then as motherhood through the Holy Spirit.

These words express the reality of the first stage of motherhood, from which its development derives: the gifts of grace, intertwined with the human gifts and without taking away their distinctiveness, perfect and strengthen the gifts and qualities of the person.

The two levels of maturity enlighten one another and are integrated. The “poor” recalls the serene reality of married life, in the joyful love of the family. But “poor” and “ugly” is the language of a humble person who recognizes herself as such, no longer by reference to a worldly value, but to the Wealth and Beauty of the All, of her Good, “the Being of her life,” the sole reason of her life.

Mother Rosa herself completed the thought by saying: “Even poor children, even if they have an ugly and poor mother, still love her … and prefer her to a princess and a noblewoman of the earth.” This is because children have a pure heart and a clear vision of life, without hypocrisy or falsehood. Rosa Gattorno’s motherhood therefore develops on two levels, human and spiritual, in two stages of life toward fullness.

Aware of this gift, she will always speak to her Daughters, and only, as a mother. Toward the end of her life she will tell them:

“I love you, my daughters, but in God, in that immense love that remains in all hearts.”7

In the depth of the gift

Rosa’s vocation obviously fits into the great and wonderful plan of salvation of the Father. Like every creature, she is freely called, by God’s grace, in the intimacy of her heart, in a dialogue of communion with God, in the mystery of the divine “You,” through a strong and indefinable love: a divine attraction that corresponds to the deepest aspirations of every human being.8

Rosa was sensitive to the transcendent. The faith in God that she had known as a girl in her family, through her mother’s good example and teaching, grew stronger and developed throughout her life. Rosa’s faith became a relationship of devotion and obedience, an orientation toward the values of honesty, integrity and goodness, in seeking and practicing that good which God had planned for her.

2.1 Vocational orientation

Rosa Gattorno left no written records of the first period of her life that could have given us useful information. We therefore cannot penetrate the intimacy of her soul, where the mutual convergence of communion took place, in the dynamism of call and consent, up to Rosa’s radical decision to obey God’s will. The development and duration of this period cannot be defined. From certain events of her childhood and adolescence, from her habitual behavior in her relationships with her family and with others, and from various conversations, one can grasp only some reflections of her inner world, of the feelings of her heart.9

At the age of eleven she received First Communion and the sacrament of Confirmation. Rosa perceived the Eucharistic experience and the gift of the Holy Spirit as something wonderful, marvelous and joyful: a mysterious fascination of light that opened her conscience to the Truth. Her mother noticed these feelings and kept them in her heart, rejoicing for her beloved daughter.10

From then on Rosa oriented herself toward the Christian values of faith, prayer and Love. She prays and teaches others to pray; she learns the catechism and teaches it to her younger brothers. She is sensitive to the needs of those who live near her, and she helps others by anticipating their needs. She “sees” the poor and helps them. With tact, kindness, love, grace and the enthusiasm of a “well-brought-up” girl, she prepares to become a good and reliable mother of a family. Her adolescence passed without upheavals, because her parents fostered the development of her identity, guiding her in the choice of existential values that could help her both in her own formation and in her relationships with her friends and peers. Her first orientation to prayer and faith led her to live these values in everyday life, guiding all her actions. Her choice to follow God’s values was tested by some non-believers who visited her family; her values were neither weakened nor altered by this experience. On the contrary, instead of weakening her, becoming familiar with the ideas and values of non-believers strengthened her faith, a faith also founded on reason.11 By the end of her adolescence her personal identity was clearly defined: “God’s calls” and her answer to him were by now certainly converging.

2.2 The choice: Marriage

But the fundamental choice raised further questions: What was her role, according to God’s plan, in her life, in society and in the Church? What life was she called to: consecrated virginity or marriage? She felt a certain inclination toward religious life. She confided her feelings and her questions about the future to persons who could help her to clarify the consistency of her intentions, first of all her parents. She reflected, prayed, and let herself be enlightened. In the end she decided for marriage, in obedience to God’s will as manifested by the mediators of his will. On 5 December 1852 she married Gerolamo Custo.

She left her parents’ home, and now she had a home of her own. She experienced the presence of God in her husband’s faithful love. She felt surrounded by the Father’s providence and goodness, which filled her life with happiness and joy; she saw peace, serenity and joy grow. She became a mother three times: at twenty-five her first child, Carlotta, was born (1853), followed by Alessandro (1855) and Francesco (1857).

2.3 “Motherhood”

The experience of motherhood, the mysterious contact with life at its sources, the unique relationship with other beings sustained by her own nourishment and entrusted to her as a precious gift to defend, care for, develop and help to grow, opened to Rosa Gattorno the immense warmth of life. The deep bonds established between Mother Rosa and her children are unforgettable. A woman’s inner world is a humanity rich in “spirituality,” in emotions and in free and conscious sharing. A mother has with the human being living within her a relationship of love, acceptance and affectionate attention: on this relationship the specifically human aspect of motherhood is founded. In it a very complex dimension creates bonds between mother and child and reaches the roots of the unconscious becoming conscious; these bonds are sublimated and remain forever.

These bonds become conscious, become spiritual, acquire value, and become permanent bonds.12 The period of gestation, of an intimate, symbiotic relationship between mother and child, is the foundation of motherhood. For nine months a vital process of symbiosis takes place, in which the mother seems a prisoner of her own perfection, and life cannot emerge from her without wounds or changes.13

But even after the child begins his or her own life with birth, the mother continues to care for the child, in a new kind of relationship, a spiritual relationship, no less important than the biological one.

To take care of a child, to give him love, to offer security and stability, to educate him, to share in his destiny: this is the normal dimension of every human motherhood. To understand the mother’s life experience, to understand the feelings of love, to assert one’s own abilities in order to be recognized for one’s own merits, to claim one’s own rights until one becomes an autonomous adult: this is the essence of the filial relationship. Therefore every mother, if she truly wishes to be a mother, must listen attentively, one might say, to the teaching of her little one, so that the child may make the difficult journey toward adult maturity.

This is why motherhood is a process that continues throughout life and extends into the gift of spiritual motherhood, in the effort to give the child one’s own spiritual life, as one gave the body, up to the total and sublime gift of self to a child accepted as distinct from oneself.14

Collapse of family life

The experience of sharing in God’s love, expressed in the gift of life to her children, in the joy of the newly formed family, was soon replaced by the opposite experience of sorrow and separation.

A first financial setback, overcome with courage and sacrifice, was soon followed by Gerolamo’s illness and his death on 9 March 1858, at the age of thirty-one. Three months later the little Francesco died. It was a terrible collapse. Rosa was devastated, almost inert, with no will to live. She was a widow at twenty-seven, poor, in the middle of quarrels over money between her parents and her parents-in-law; even her furniture was seized. She gratefully accepted her father’s offer and returned to the Gattorno family home, the house she had left six years earlier, when she had been welcomed with joy by her husband and had dreamed of the happiness of her family, of an intimate and lasting love. With her faith, Rosa overcame her resentment at her in-laws’ unjust behavior, and, although she was the greatest victim of the conflict, she made peace. She built peace, for love of God and also for the sake of her innocent children, who had a right to life, to joy, to the happiness of a family life. With a “supplementary” love she tried to fill the void left by their father’s death, providing a climate of security and balance; she also tried to harmonize the role of the paternal grandparents and to restore normal family relationships.

The reunited family looked to the future with optimism and hope, sustained by the financial help of “Dad” Francesco and by Rosa’s spiritual richness. With her calm, reasonable and cheerful attitude she created a positive climate and a warm, loving and new family life, founded on relationships of love, acceptance, trust and mutual affection. Rosa had become the heart of hope for her children and for her parents, who felt her to be part of their life and a support for the future.

3. Toward a broader horizon

Struck by the harshness of the cross, Rosa tried to understand its meaning. By spending much time in prayer, contemplating Christ crucified, the only one without sin, she was able to find meaning in all her sufferings, and this understanding enlightened her. A new life began in her soul. Her motherhood, born of sacramental love through human bonds, sought a new extension, with no limits of quantity or space. Christ’s command, “love one another as I have loved you,” developed in her soul a new capacity to love and urged her to dedicate her life to Christ and to her brothers and sisters.

She served her brothers and sisters through an apostolic action inspired by the Holy Spirit. The “method” born of the heart of Christ, who invented a thousand ways to express his tenderness and did good to everyone even to the point of dying on the Cross, was for Rosa a call to go beyond the boundaries of her own family and paternal home, to reach the broader horizon of the family of God, authentically represented by the local Church and by her own parish.

3.1 A new vocational call

In this context Rosa discovers the open field of charity and explores it where the cry of weakness and poverty is strongest:

“… Having been left free of every bond, I devoted myself with greater fervor to pious works and to visiting the hospitals and the poor sick in their homes, helping them by assisting them as much as I could and serving them in everything. [With] the grace of the Lord I realized that all earthly affections were dissipating; nothing was any longer pleasing to me, only my God was the pasture of all my delights.”15

The “Memoirs” are spiritual writings and contain mostly autobiographical information. These words, with which the Memoirs begin, are a great revelation. From 1858, after her husband’s death, Rosa is free to make a free choice: “I devoted myself,” “visiting”; and her attitude toward God and human affairs is completely different: “nothing was any longer pleasing to me, only my God was the pasture of all my delights.” The language is clear and explicit: it is an experience of knowing God, in the face of which everything loses importance. A very severe regime of fasting and penance began; Rosa wished to make God the center of her whole life. She strengthened a relationship of trust and love with Mary, the Mother of Jesus:

“I received great graces from Most Holy Mary. During the novena under the title of Our Lady of the Vineyards, while the Blessed Sacrament was exposed for Benediction, I saw in the Most Holy Host the living Blood that seemed to be poured out; what this sight produced in me I cannot express: a union, a fire that consumed me.”16

3.2 A bride of her Good

Rosa was clearly aware of God’s total call. She felt deeply her own unworthiness, as a void to be filled: “It is truly nothing to give him all of ourselves, compared with so great an immensity of grandeur.”17 Rosa consecrates her whole life to God, through Mary:

“I was granted to make the perpetual vow of chastity, poverty and obedience, and I laid everything at the feet of Mary, that she might make a gift of it to my Good Jesus and beg him to accept me as his bride.”18 Her life changes radically. In four years she attains a strong spiritual maturity and can truly say: “I no longer live; it is you who live for me.”19

She wishes to follow Jesus totally: “O eternal Love, you suffered so much for me: grant that I may suffer and die for you.”20

She does not stop; she will not turn back: “Only Calvary, I know, is the safe mountain on which to rest.”21

Rosa wishes to give her life to God and “her blood in exchange for the blood of Jesus.”22

Prayer is her greatest comfort and her irresistible resource. She prayed for many hours before the Blessed Sacrament, at night at home and also in church. Often, while adoring the Eucharistic Host, she fell into ecstasy. As a free gift, God granted her the revelation of the mysterious “Sign” of the Father’s merciful love.

“I saw the most precious Blood of my Lord and rejoiced in it. What did this sight make me feel? Oh, my Love, I can only say that you worked a spiritual miracle in my soul: I was caught up in ecstasy and could say nothing. Besides, very little can be said to a God so merciful.”23 Dwelling in God in an attitude of prayer and adoration, she exclaims: “Oh, you who are my Paradise, what can I do to make you known to the whole world! Oh, how many there are who do not know you, and those who have known you flee from you because they have never seen you. I would like to run everywhere and cry out loudly for everyone to come [and] love you.”24

She becomes a heart that loves as God loves: “Oh, why does everyone not love you!”

She said nothing to anyone about her new “form of life”; but her behavior, her attitude, her inclination to communion with God, and her desire to help the poor and the needy revealed it.

3.3 Converging lines toward a new form of life

Rosa took part in various Christian associations, which were very active in Genoa at that time. They were promoted by excellent priests, who encouraged the growth of faith in its various aspects of worship, religious instruction and the practice of charity. Rosa discovered in them an immense field of work: hours of Eucharistic adoration, the spread of the good press, the instruction of youth in Christian doctrine, the protection of “endangered girls” and other works of charity.

Rosa distinguished herself among all the other charity workers by the unconditional gift of her time and energies, by her perseverance and by her fidelity to the aims of these associations.

A problem that concerned her closely and urgently, as a mother, was that of the “endangered girls.” Many girls came to Genoa looking for work and to escape poverty.

Unfortunately many of them were young and inexperienced, and they always ended up as victims of unscrupulous exploiters. Strength and commitment were needed to help and save them. Rosa succeeded in communicating this sense of urgency to her more active and sensitive friends. A small group of “committed” ladies, almost all married and mothers, took shape and became a small religious “family,” with regular meetings, ideals, aims and its own norms of spiritual life. They called themselves “Ursulines,” following a custom widespread in Genoa for lay ladies who lived in the world according to a religious rule for laypeople.25

Rosa Gattorno was elected superior by all the members of the association. After a year’s trial the Archbishop, Msgr. Charvaz, officially approved the new association, confirmed the superior’s appointment and entrusted the spiritual direction of the community to Canon Fr. Luigi Botto. This was at the end of 1864.

In February 1864, at the explicit wish of the Archbishop himself, Rosa Gattorno was appointed General President of the “Pious Union of the Daughters of Mary Immaculate,” founded by Fr. Giuseppe Frassinetti to guide its members, who remained in their own families, toward a Christian life solidly based on spiritual growth and on the practice of the evangelical virtues and of charity. The Union had spread in Genoa and its surroundings. The Founder had written the Rule and presented it for the Archbishop’s approval; not having yet obtained it, he asked Rosa Gattorno to act as mediator, hoping for a favorable outcome both because she was an excellent president and because of the great esteem the pastor had for her. The Archbishop explained to Rosa the reasons for the refusal: some points needed to be corrected, and, to her great surprise, he invited her to suggest the appropriate corrections herself, by guessing which points of the Rule he disapproved of.

She accepted the invitation obediently. In a spirit of prayer and reflection she noted down the corrections that she understood needed to be made; she thanked her Good and continued to contemplate Christ crucified. At a certain moment she received the inspiration to write something else, something very different: she wrote brief notes of “monastic Rules,” then folded the sheet and continued to pray. She did not know, nor did she care to ask, what would happen next. The spark of life inspired Mother Rosa at an unforeseen moment and in an unforeseen event, which she had not anticipated and which was beyond her control: she could not decide “when” it would happen. Life was born in her, but it did not originate from her.

4. The Work of God

In 1864, while she was superior of the growing “Society of the Ursulines,” Rosa Gattorno had reflected on the possibility of following the consecrated life while living in her own family, harmonizing the needs of the family with the practice of works of charity outside the home.

She had noticed the difficulties met by her fellow sisters, the obstacles, the delays, the dissatisfaction in carrying out works of charity, the lack of answers to the needs of the poor.

Yet she had never thought of leaving her father’s house, which she now considered her own home, or her elderly parents and her children.

But the source of life that God had entrusted to her as a gift in that night of prayer demanded the right to be born. In spite of her reluctance, she had to take those notes for the foundation of a monastic community and submit them to her spiritual director, Fr. Firpo. What the Father told her is narrated in the Memoirs: she was rebuked for the delay in obeying God’s will and was told to go at once to the Archbishop. The Archbishop urged her to “carry out the Lord’s commands,” because he saw that the Work would certainly be most beautiful, and he encouraged her to write the Rule.26

The charismatic vocation

Rosa Gattorno had sought and obeyed God’s will when she chose the vocation to marriage. And God had blessed her marriage with the gift of children, for whom, according to the Gospel, she would have to give account. Was God now contradicting himself by asking her to leave them? She faced a grave dilemma. Was it possible that she was receiving a new vocational call from God? Was that “Work” truly willed by God, or was it the work of the devil? If God wanted the Work to succeed, could it not be accomplished by another person? In the immense sorrow of her mother’s heart she turned to the heart of the Holy Father, Pius IX. The Holy Father could have released her from that obedience; instead he confirmed to her that the Work was God’s will! And with the light she also received the courage to reaffirm the positive answer of her Christian life:

“No, Holy Father, I want to do the will of God.”27

4.2 Spiritual motherhood

“In so cruel a battle” she had hoped for “peace and relief” from the Vicar of Christ. “The balm on the wound of sorrow, bitterly opened,” was applied by Mary:

“I must abandon my children! Your Son commands it of me through his Vicar! I feel torn apart by sorrow; I am so deeply attached to them! […] Leave them? And where? And with whom? Alas, it is too much! […] Mary, Mary, my mother, what a knife this is; it pierces me to the marrow of my bones! I remained absorbed; my tears dried up, and in the Most Holy Virgin I found peace and strength.

When I came to myself, I found myself transformed, a giant. With generosity I made God the offering of it and repeated to him the words of Abraham: Here I am to do your divine will.”28

At the feet of the holy Mother, torn by sorrow, she felt transformed into a spiritual giant and experienced the great peace and joy of her motherhood, which brings salvation to all. The human dimension of her motherhood now opened to a greater spiritual dimension: a gift neither sought nor wanted, but given by the pure mercy of God.

In the spirit of the faith of Abraham and of Mary, she took part in the blessed generation accomplished in Mary, whom Rosa “loved and venerated.”

4.2.1 Sharing in the motherhood-fatherhood of God

Rosa Gattorno was able to experience the merciful love of the Father in the contemplation of Christ crucified, who prolongs his “Memorial” in the Eucharist. In the vision, which she had several times, of the Blood of Christ appearing on the Host, she lived an irresistible religious experience. God the Father redeemed her soul through the Blood of the Son, and she, a daughter in the Son, entered into the experience of the Most Holy Trinity, which she called “the Essence of Love.” Among the various passages of this experience, this one is very significant:

“O eternal Father! You yourself communicate yourself to me in this communion, offering me your divine Son as you offered him for the salvation of all humanity, that he may purify all my senses and free me entirely from their slavery, and grant me your mercy. I am a servant who obeys your will; I want to be always your servant: grant that I may be fulfilled in the essence of your love. With your gentle hands give me Jesus. Yes, you are the only Being of my life, you are my all, because when I have you I have everything from you… I have everything.”29

Something has happened in the soul of Rosa Gattorno, and she expresses it exactly in her prayer: in her own way she repeats the Magnificat of Mary. The Almighty has done great things in her: he has made her share in the mystery of Christ’s salvation. She feels unworthy of this gift. In her poverty as a sinner she asks to be involved in it, “…you communicate yourself to me in this communion,” because she longs to draw near to God; she wants to be a servant bound to the mercy of God; she desires nothing else. She has discovered her beatitude, her only Good. With clear awareness she proclaims her total belonging to God: “Yes, you are the only Being of my life, you are my all, because when I have you I have everything.”30

Here Rosa reaches the zenith of her own awareness of God: she, who is nothing, receives her “Being” from the Father. If God did not remain close to her, Rosa, his creature, would fall back into nothingness. She was nothing if she relied only on her own resources; she needed the strength that only God can give for her apostolic work, and the love and security that only God could offer her. With these gifts she felt completely safe, like a little girl in her mother’s arms. God the Father was for her “infinite justice, infinite mercy, infinite love, the joy of her soul, infinite power, her delight, her refuge, the One who gives her everything, who stretches out his gentle hand over her, guardian and light of her daughters, the only Being of her life, her all.”

Mother Rosa comes to this experience through the historical stages of her life as a woman: first a girl, then a fiancée, a wife, a mother and a widow. What gift did God wish to give to this woman, fulfilled in her human and spiritual life? He granted her his living and personal presence; he helped her, who was already a mother, to become even more active and fruitful in the lives of others, through her belonging to God, wholly God’s and living for God.

“Motherhood” qualifies not only the mission but also the consecration of her spiritual Daughters. Their fundamental attitude of faith in the poor and liberating Christ has its roots in Christ the Son of the Father, who obeyed the Father’s will by dying, and dying on the cross, because he loved the Father. To speak of a filial attitude is to speak of the Trinity and of the Trinitarian relationship, in the dynamic dimension of a love that has the traits of fatherhood. “In the biblical tradition God does not reveal himself only in masculine language; the feminine dimension too is an instrument of God’s revelation.

God and Christ are personified in the feminine themes of wisdom (Prov 8:22-26; Sir 24:9; 1 Cor 1:24, 30). God is also compared to a mother who comforts her children (Is 66:13) and to a mother who cannot forget her baby (Is 49:15; Ps 25:6; 116:5). Jesus compares himself to a mother who wants to gather her children under her protection (Lk 13:34). And at the end of the Church’s pilgrimage on earth, God will act as a great and good Mother: he will wipe away the tears from our eyes, weary from so much weeping (Rev 21:4). Every element of tenderness, welcome and hospitality in the definitive refuge of God’s salvation is presented in the tradition in feminine language.”31

The Savior entered the human world through the “yes” of Mary. Through the mystery of the Incarnation she is in an intimate relationship with the Father, who makes her share in his original creative power; she has an intimate relationship with the Son, who accomplishes in Mary and through Mary his historical, human life; she has an intimate relationship with the Holy Spirit, the divine force that regenerates the human reality of the eternal Son in Mary’s womb.32 The Trinity touches Mary deeply: “God chose her to manifest the maternal aspect of his person: generosity, goodness, tenderness, the feminine traits, the traits of a mother. The Virgin is the person in whom the Holy Spirit is present, just as the Child Jesus is the Person in whom the Word is present. The two together make the mysterious presence of the Father understandable to human beings.”33

4.3 The dynamism of the new motherhood

How did Mother Rosa live her participation in Mary’s maternal destiny? Mother Rosa was inspired and struck by “her beauty, her power and the love she bears for us, poor and miserable creatures.”34

Rosa entrusted herself completely to Mary: “Mary, Mary! You are my life!”,35 that she might belong completely and forever only to Jesus, transformed and enlightened by his love. She asked Mary: “loose the chains of this poor creature […] give me only love! […] Ah, become my teacher and teach me what I must do to become less displeasing to my dear Jesus.”36 Mother Rosa feels herself regenerated in Mary’s “Fiat,” sharing in her universal motherhood. In contemplation she clarifies and deepens her awareness of her own participation in Mary’s maternal function in the plan of salvation:

“O Mary, through you I am saved, through you I am a religious! The fire of your Son’s love, Mary, you kindled many times with your hands in this heart. Oh yes, love! Why do you not make me die of it?”37

From Mary she received the great gift of Mary’s Mother, St. Anne: “With great pleasure I dedicate this Work to my Mother.”38 With the holy Mother she receives the specific charism, the spirituality and also the mission of her Daughters. The Daughters are the historical descendants of the blessed Family of Anne and Joachim, as a sign and instrument of the Father’s mercy, in the motherhood that strengthens, serves, makes life grow and consoles the world.39 In the passionate gift of herself to her crucified Good, she accepts forgiveness and the saving power of suffering in compassion (“suffering with”), lived in her affective life and in her flesh, through a “more concrete love” made of deeds; and it is at the same time a tangible and trusting abandonment, by inspiration of the Holy Spirit, into the arms of the Father, lived in the trials of suffering and of the “thousand” contradictions of everyday life:

“Of everything I made an offering to God, of my sufferings, and enclosed in him his poor slave lived, if one could call it living, because only my Master, my All, I can assure you, led me like a little child.”40

Mother Rosa lives the dynamism of her charismatic mission with enthusiasm and an ardor never satisfied, offering the gift of the Father’s merciful love, fully manifested in the crucified Son: to live only for the Work of God. She wanted to belong to everyone, to welcome everyone, with humility and with “charity without limits and without reward,” in an attitude of peace, strength and serenity. She made herself available to all, acting as a mother, so that Christ, the living image of the Father, might extend, through her maternal cooperation, his tenderness to the “beloved” of this world: those who suffer in flesh and spirit, the poorest children, young people in difficulty, the elderly and all the others. She also intended to form the Daughters of St. Anne as true, active and creative members of the Family willed by the Father in the Church, helping them to become aware of the vocational charism; she wished the family to bear fruits of holiness, serving and stimulating the growth of a holy spiritual life.

With a mother’s heart, a “compassionate” heart that expressed God’s maternal tenderness, Mother Rosa wanted her Daughters to live with authentic hope, hastening and preparing the coming of the Kingdom of God, the fulfillment of every expectation and the proof that God’s promise is true and trustworthy. Mother Rosa reached this dimension of spiritual motherhood through a process of purification and trial; enriched by her conjugal and maternal experience, she matured harmoniously into a new and more intense vital dynamism. She founded her faith on certainty and trusted in her only Good, Jesus crucified, the Being of her life.

RELATIONSHIP OF MOTHERHOOD

The twofold function of motherhood

The resolve to give her whole life to Christ, without regrets or limits of time, “from this moment, for the rest of my life, your bride seeks only to suffer and to do what you and the Father want of me,”41 meant for Rosa Gattorno being constantly attentive to God’s will, now walking the path of uncertainty and adventure, without any fear of pain and of the cross.

God was calling her to accomplish his Work. Her obedient “yes,” confirmed by the Holy Father Pius IX, was a commitment she could not renounce. Mother Rosa wrote:

“I repeated to him the words of Abraham: Here I am to do your divine will. And I never again returned to complaints and almost insistent attempts to go back, and to a thousand protests. Offered as a victim for his Work, I received very great consolations, and the Most Holy Virgin assured me that she will always be with me and that my children will be hers.”42

God guided her with the wonderful pedagogy of love:

“I have been taught by my eternal Father, and in everything I have done according to his will I have succeeded.”43

And she followed his will, docile to the grace of the Holy Spirit:

“In all truth I can say that I no longer feel alive, but in him I live.”44

In this dimension of transcendence she sought to be docile in loving others; she sought to be a reflection of the Father’s mercy and tenderness, welcoming the littleness of all God’s creatures. What did the Father command her? To love God! This love for God, which urged her to love her brothers and sisters, “was not a bond, but only the consequence of having followed the command received from God.”45

God was in her heart a source of life for her brothers and sisters. Every day Rosa let herself be taught and guided by the Spirit, expressing her gift of motherhood. For this reason she was able to understand God’s thoughts about her own children. At first the children seem a great obstacle to God’s call to accomplish his Work: “I love them too much, I cannot leave them; Holy Father, it is impossible!”

Can God contradict himself? “Oh no, Holy Father, according to the holy Gospel God will ask me to account for my children!”46

The Pope’s answer, which she interpreted in a context of separation (nor could it be otherwise), actually had a meaning that she understood only later: “God will take care of your children; you take care of God in his Work.”47 What a true prophecy!

The love of God manifested in her womb had become God’s gift for her three children. Did God’s love perhaps exclude them from her heart by asking her to attain a spiritual maturity extended to the dimensions of a gift without limits? St. Vincent de Paul wrote a gentle rebuke to Louise de Marillac, who was excessively worried about her son’s fate and believed she was obeying God’s will even though she was too anxious about him:

“Oh, truly Our Lord did well not to want you for his mother, since you do not believe you are doing God’s will by giving your son the maternal care he requires! Or perhaps you think this task prevents you from doing God’s will. Honor, then, the tranquility of the Blessed Virgin in a similar case.”48

Rosa Gattorno experienced, like Louise de Marillac and some other foundresses of religious Orders, widows and mothers of children of their own, the contradiction of a radical change in the direction of her life.

At certain moments, above all when the obstacles to the approval of the Rules seemed insurmountable and no one wanted to recognize the legitimacy of the Institute’s charismatic inspiration, she felt the temptation to abandon everything and return to her children:

“I receive everything from the hands of God. Only one thing pains me: my boys. Giggino’s letter threw me to the ground. Wretched me, what have I done?”49

She was worried also about the fate of Carlotta and Alessandro; yet she never doubted that she was obeying God’s will in caring so much for her own children. Her mission of motherhood, begun in marriage, had developed through the gift of her children and had then extended to a religious Family, formed by her spiritual Daughters. Her children were, and remained, very important to Mother Rosa.

When she presented to the Pope the proposal of a new religious Order, her children were living in boarding school. She did not hesitate to take Carlotta out of the institute in Piacenza when the directress informed her that cholera had broken out there. Her mother’s heart had already generously taken in many children orphaned by the cholera epidemic. Later she sent Carlotta to a boarding school in Milan, where she was educated by an excellent teacher, Onorata Colli, who was also one of the first lay collaborators in the foundation of the new religious Family of the Daughters of St. Anne. In the depth of the call to spiritual maturity, God had reminded her to take care of her own children, because this was certainly his will. She was sure of it, and she expressed it to Maria Adelaide, Carlotta’s firstborn:

“Naughty girl, how can you believe such things? How can you believe that your grandmother forgets you? Oh, you really are a strange creature! If you knew how many prayers I say for all those of my family, how many prayers I undertake to say! So what should I do? Pray and write to everyone; but first my duty to the Work of God.”50

There was, then, a priority: “for the Work of her heart I would give, and I gave, all that I had and finally life itself, under continual suffering and pains of every kind.”51 But priority did not mean exclusion. Her children were children of God even before being her children. God had wanted them, had always loved them in his plan of salvation and had entrusted them to her. They too were part, and what an important part!, of the small, poor and sick life that God entrusted to her service of motherhood.

2. Rosa Gattorno in the filial relationship

To enter the “maternal world” of Rosa Gattorno we have reliable and very important historical sources. Among the documents on which our research is based, the most important, because of their exceptional value, are the letters written by Rosa Gattorno to her children: letters addressed to Carlotta and her family,52 to Alessandro and to the Daughters of St. Anne.

In her letters to her family Mother Rosa wrote with the strength of her decisive, clear and essential style, and openly revealed her thoughts and feelings. She was spontaneous and lively. Her letters are like shafts of light which, despite the distance of time, make her present, relevant, almost alive even today. They reveal her feelings, her ideas, her moral stature and her most intimate thoughts, which could be described as a beautiful and immensely rich “house.”

In the long-distance relationship with her children attested by the correspondence, she reveals her capacity to love. Care, respect, responsibility and understanding are traits she showed throughout her life as a mother. To have access to the documents that describe her intimate relationship with her children is for us a gift and a charism: a gift that she was able to communicate to us, developed by her love for her children and by the strength of that love, which draws us into her great capacity to love others.

3. Relationship with her children

3.1 With Carlotta

Between Rosa and Carlotta there was a relationship of empathy, with deep spiritual resources. Rosa loved her daughter in the Spirit of her “Good” and desired that she grow free, mature and blessed by the Lord. She wrote to her: “Love Jesus very much, my daughter, let him be your only thought, Jesus your beloved spouse, all yours.” Rosa paid great attention to Carlotta and satisfied her small wishes: “Tomorrow I will send you the dress, which is already finished. I spoke to your grandfather about the clock, and tomorrow, when I go to Genoa again, I will see that he buys it for you; I will bring it to you myself…”53

The human love of this mother, “conquered by Christ,” drew strength from the love of God and developed a motherhood so rich that it embraced the whole earthly life of her daughter. Attention, time and faithfulness converged on her: an uninterrupted gift of strength, security, love and life. Love and life are the two foci that bound mother and daughter together in a continuous relationship. Mother Rosa’s letters offer clear testimony of it. The strong and tender expressions she uses reveal not only the quality of a love that transcends life in God, but also a love strengthened by her paternal and maternal tenderness. They reveal, too, her concerns, her interest in concrete situations, her timely interventions and the lines of a maternal pedagogy, wise because enlightened by her intimate communion with God.

A pedagogy of love that:

Makes her grow

Her daughter was not to experience loneliness and her mother’s absence. So Rosa made up for her long absences, caused by her frequent journeys from one community to another, with letters and an affectionate dialogue, explaining how her activity differed from that of other mothers, something the girl could not always accept or fully understand. From Nizza, on 7 September 1874, she wrote to Carlotta:

“My dear little Carlotta, why are you so cross with me? Think how busy I am: I do nothing but write […]. Then I will tell you everything. You say, ‘Poor me!’; instead you should say, ‘Poor Mamma.’ Today, as I write to you, I have such a bad headache that even my nerves curl up, and I am alone, ‘poor Mamma’; you are well and are enjoying yourself with Onorata. Be calm, for here there is nothing to enjoy…

I cannot wait for the moment to leave, and I hope to go to Ovada on Saturday, or Monday at the latest. I pass through Acqui because, as you know, I must see the Bishop; then I will not come back to Nizza, but go straight from Acqui to Ovada by the same road. You, who have nothing to do and nothing to think about, imagine that it is the same for me…”54

Healthy growth

Carlotta was thirteen when, in 1867, she was admitted as a boarder in Piacenza. She suffered from deafness, which prevented normal and serene relationships. Disturbed and incomplete communication affected her character, making her often moody, aggressive, suspicious and sad. Once her distress took a form that worried Mother Rosa greatly, and she wrote about it sadly to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa on 5 February 1869:

“It is eight days since Carlotta fell ill, with a rather strange and frightening illness. My dear, she is like a madwoman, and neither I nor your [sister] can leave her bedside. Angiola too. Many times, when she is in a fury, not even four of us can hold her; she lashes out with her fists at everything. My Jesus, I assure you that this cup is very bitter for this poor mother! The doctor assures me that she will recover and that it is not madness, but first he had leeches applied, saying it was a congestion of blood in the brain; now he says it is ‘nervous irritation,’ but all the same dear little Carlotta is not getting better. Prayers, candles. On Sunday she was so furious that Father had to stay and sleep here.

What do you make of it? Now it is very late, and she has been resting for two hours, now and then letting out a cry. Last night Father stayed again, and I had to be at her bed all the time, such was her fury; so did your sister. I feel ill; I have vomiting that is killing me. I cannot take anything. There you have my wretched situation. May the Lord be blessed forever!…”55

In the early years Rosa took Carlotta with her to the various communities when she had to stay there for many days. On 25 August 1869, writing from Genoa to Carolina Pezzoni, she expressed her apprehension about “the little cut they have to make on Carlotta’s knee” and recommended: “First of all, speak to Father about it and have her blessed.”56

Was Carlotta, like Alessandro, predisposed to lung disease? There was an episode that alarmed Mother Rosa and deeply disturbed her. She wrote to her son-in-law Gaspare on 22 February 1881:

“I urge you to take great care of Carla, that she not worry, because, as the time approaches when the blood came from her mouth, it could certainly return. I am anxious.”

She gives strength

Carlotta’s case therefore involved elements to be considered seriously. Mother Rosa rightly said: “What anguish this thought gives me! All of them, one after another, form a heap.” Her intelligent mind understood her daughter’s situation. She loved, she anticipated and she prayed. She did not dramatize the small gestures by which her daughter expressed not so much disapproval as deep suffering. What went on in the heart of a thirteen-year-old girl on seeing her mother surrounded by so many young women whom she loved, served wholeheartedly, educated and called daughters? What did Carlotta think of her mother’s decision to leave her in order to follow her spiritual Daughters?

One day, while her mother was writing to one of those young women, Carlotta came up and read: “dear Caterina, my daughter.” That word was too much: she could not write it! Was she not the true daughter? Mother Rosa simply explained to the recipient why the word “daughter” had been crossed out: “you can imagine who crossed out daughter: it was dear little Carlotta.” Could Rosa’s daughter take seriously certain things her mother said about her relationship with the other Daughters, so deep that she dreamed of them? The other Daughters had made a different choice, and Mother Rosa told them of the new and wonderful life of the Family of St. Anne. From Cento she writes to the superior of the community in Piacenza:

“Nothing new; we can only pray. This night I stayed with Daria. All the little sleep I got was very little; I was happy there; she held me in her lap. It is a dream, and Carlotta says: they are lies.”57

She gives understanding and joy

These small daily episodes show, with great simplicity and spontaneity, not only Carlotta’s latent suffering but also her firm and resolute character: she was a Gattorno, after all. In the environment of the Family of St. Anne, rich in human and Christian values, she grew up “good” and “religious,” honest, and she learned, by looking at her mother with unlimited trust, to overcome the weak sides of her personality and to shape her own character by following her mother’s positive model. Friendship with some of the Sisters was a positive experience for her: she was a friend of Vincenza Rapallino (the girl of the letter in which she had crossed out, in annoyance, the word “daughter”), of Benedetta Carrega and of other Sisters, and she enjoyed the friendship of girls whose education and culture suited her condition. When she confided to her mother that she had fallen in love and wanted to marry the man who loved her, her mother did not oppose it at all: although anxious about her marriage, she gave her consent. Rosa trusted her daughter: her heart told her that Carlotta would be a wonderful wife and a good mother. She knew, however, that Carlotta would always need her help.

Carlotta remained marked for life by the handicap of deafness, which often had a negative effect on her physical health as well. Her mother, the only one who knew the true cause of her pessimism and distrust, repeated the same message to her in almost every letter and on every occasion:

“Be cheerful! I do not want melancholy to take hold of you! Cheer up, dear Carlotta… my daughter, you are really a child, to be upset because I write to Nonni (dear Maria Adelaide) and not to you. Oh, what a creature you are! Do not be cross about it; be cheerful… I do not want you to be sad, no! no! I say it because melancholy does no good; I do not like it.”58 “How can you doubt that I love you little? Oh, what a girl! Never doubt that I love you far too much; is it not so? See what I ever do for you?”59

Carlotta’s distrust arose from melancholy and apathy, which could have subtly destroyed her. Her mother stayed close to her with the affectionate love of her wonderful humanity and with her gifts of grace. In 1880 Mother Rosa wrote to Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega:

“…Poor girl, one day she will know the love her mother bears her. My God, I would feel guilty if I had not done so much to help her!”

The letters we examine and quote were not written with specifically pedagogical aims. They were signs of the love of a distant mother, deeply immersed in the world and in the field of work that belongs to God, who traveled and visited the communities of the Daughters of St. Anne. Carlotta would have liked her mother’s love to be wholly for her, more than for the Sisters, and would have liked her to give her more time. In reading these letters one grasps the outline of a simple, clear and consistent pedagogy which, while accompanying the married life chosen by Carlotta, remained centered on God, as a vocation to live one’s baptismal consecration as a lay woman who puts the reality of God’s will at the center of her life and work.

She guides and supports

Carlotta, as wife and mother, had precise responsibilities. Mother Rosa reminds her of them with gentleness and with the firm insistence of one who had lived that experience and had not merely heard about it.

Fortunately for Carlotta, the peace and joy that came to her from her husband’s love helped her to develop a more positive image of herself, as we have already seen. The care of her health was also an important subject. Some quotations from Mother Rosa’s letters show the tone of her advice:

“…I hear that you are not very well; what is the matter? Why do you not eat? Cheer up, for I am settling what I can in order to come away.

I will be in Naples only a very short time; so if you want me to come soon and bring you a lovely present, I want to hear that you eat plenty, that you are cheerful and that you are putting on weight; then you will see what Mamma will do… It seems to me I have not seen you for so long… Take care of yourself; let me know whether you are eating, whether you are cheerful.”60

“Dear Carlotta, yesterday I received your letter with such joy. Thank you, you are a good daughter! See that you take care of yourself. I would like to know whether you are really well again. Look after yourself.”

Mother Rosa did not ask about her daughter’s health out of mere curiosity. She was anxious about her son Alessandro, who had pulmonary tuberculosis, the same disease that had caused his father’s death. Alessandro was very ill, in a pitiable state; his mother wrote: “He would move stones to pity.”61 Rosa had nursed him, and Alessandro had died a year before this letter. So any illness of her daughter alarmed her: “Carlotta, write to me at once and tell me what is the matter. Take care of yourself; soon I will be with you.”62

To her son-in-law she wrote: “The news of Carlotta keeps me in continual agitation; you cannot imagine how I suffer… my God, what a sorrow!”63

Later Carlotta was out of danger, healed. Her mother comments on the event: “Carlotta, do you understand what has happened to you? Do not overtire yourself!”64

She expressed her concern for her daughter’s health:

“Dear daughter, I have received your letter and I understand that you are agitated, even though you tell me you are cheerful. Dear Carlotta, do not get angry. I would like you not to get agitated, because the spitting of blood could return, you know. So do not get angry. I hope you will come soon, is that true? I am waiting for you; come soon, because here (in Piacenza) it is no longer hot.”65

This care and fear for her daughter’s health may seem exaggerated and anxious. We know, however, that Mother Rosa did not intend to flee suffering, and always believed it bearable to suffer for the love she felt for her Good. She confided it to her dear friend, Princess Emilia di Fitalia, on 11 February 1891, from Piacenza, where she was assisting her son in the last phase of his illness:

“Pains are borne and carried willingly, but anguish is unbearable; to watch so much suffering is a terrible struggle with the humanity that always fights and always wants to win.”66

She was a mother. She lived all the normal joys and sorrows that every mother knows. She was deeply struck by the death of her beloved son Alessandro and thought it better not to speak of it to Carlotta, fearing a serious trauma for her if she learned of that premature death. Thirteen days after Alessandro’s death she confided her great sorrow to a friend:

“I do not speak of Carlotta. Who knows what my daughter is feeling, now that she is expecting a child (Carlotta was then in the fifth month of pregnancy). She wants to know everything, she weeps, she worries about her brother; I think it is better that she not come to the funeral. I need God’s strength more than ever.”67

God certainly gave her strength. On her way to Calvary, the only safe place where she could stop and regain strength was her Good, who gave her the courage she needed to go on caring for the creatures, spiritual and human, whom God had entrusted to her. He alone could help her, and he certainly did. Mother Rosa received the courage to bear all the sorrows of her life and to carry her cross to Calvary. Her goodness was selfless and generous. She always took care of the people she loved, knowing that this care concerned not only earthly life but also eternal life with God. She did not measure the time or the sacrifices she made for them. She gave everything for love of God. She always committed herself to works of charity with his approval and guidance. She had to help her own children and at the same time take care of the religious Family that she had worked so hard to found. Despite the very intense program of visits, interviews and appointments, she still found time to give care and joy to her own children and to her other relatives. Even late at night, after a day of very hard work, she thought of her family: she remembered them in her prayers and wrote to them.

“I must write, but at night, because during the day I have so many people and their needs to deal with… It is almost midnight; at last I can write to you… I am tired, I must go, I have little time to write… Read as best you can; I cannot see what I am writing because it is dark… I cannot keep my eyes open.”68

During her mother’s absences, the daughter welcomed her correspondence. Rosa wrote to Carlotta: “I write to you only a little, but I write to you every day. Are you happy?… See that you use the ear trumpet; do not neglect to use it; if you always carry it with you, you will hear well and you will be better.”69

In both Piacenza and Rome, the houses where Carlotta’s family lived were next to the motherhouse of the Daughters of St. Anne.

Exhortations and reproofs

Patience, gentleness and understanding are not signs of weakness. The sensitivity she had developed, the ability to understand problems and questions clearly and to uncover lies, hypocrisy and difficulties were gifts that Mother Rosa possessed and used effectively. She understood her own daughter even better than the mentality of the Sisters. She admonished her firmly but gently:

“I wish you would understand the sufferings of others! Then your own would seem to you things of no account, compared with the problems of others.”

With a clear eye and a pure heart she saw the confused thinking of those who tried to set her daughter against her. On 29 October 1882 she wrote to Carlotta:

“Dear Carlotta,

I have received your letter and I hear that you are not happy. Why? You say you fear that I am angry: why do you say so? For what reasons do you suppose I am angry with you? I think of you always; I am even looking for a nursemaid for you. What more could you ask? I know that no mother does for her children what I do for you; why, then, so many doubts? Whoever tells you that I do not do enough for you is a liar, or has a mind confused by prejudice. Be cheerful; I have serious worries, because I am full of debts and without much money. I have to undo so many things… do you understand what I am saying? It will be easier when I explain everything to you in person. Your affectionate Mamma now greets you.”70

In twenty-two years of marriage Carlotta had six children. So large a family demanded continual attention and effort, and Carlotta needed a great spirit of sacrifice to cope with it. At forty-three she felt exhausted and without confidence in the future, and she confided her discouragement to her mother. Mother Rosa understood the situation: the problem was not really the children, so full of life, cordial, a blessing of God. The problem was another, and Mother Rosa revealed its nature:

“You are wrong when you say: no more children. The Lord does not like it. You must be cheerful; drive away, as a temptation, the thought of not having enough money: that is what a miser does. I never think like that, though the Institute has so many needs and all the Sisters I have to support; is it not so? You too, abandon yourself to God: he will provide for all your needs. Will you do it? So be cheerful.”71

Totally abandoned in God. This is the secret of Mother Rosa’s spiritual fruitfulness: God provides for everything, because she has chosen her Good as the one thing necessary. Could her daughter understand it and live the same ideal?

Rosa returned to the subject in another letter, but without wanting to constrain Carlotta, because she trusted her judgment. Her firm conviction was expressed in love and gentleness:

“…remember that Mamma is all her Carlotta’s. Whenever you are in need and whenever you want something, you have only to tell me and you will have it, believe me. Provided it is not against fairness, for I know you to be so upright and capable of doing only good. Well done!”72

Mother Rosa knew how to draw out the best thoughts in the human soul and to set free authentically Christian thoughts:

“Dear Carlotta,

yesterday I wrote to you, now I write to you again. Be cheerful! Do you promise me to be cheerful? You must not think about anything, but put everything in God’s hands. I promise you that Jesus will always take thought for his children. So do not complain! Woe to whoever complains! Be cheerful…”73

Here “thinking” means worrying excessively about the future: an un-Christian trait, typical of those who lack faith. At this point Mother Rosa sketches for her daughter a spiritual program, the same that had been prophetically given to her by the unforgettable Pius IX:

“God will take care of your children; you take care of God in his Work.” The Pope’s prophecy had been fully fulfilled for Mother Rosa, and she assures her daughter: “Your mother promises you that Jesus will always take care of his children!”

3.1.1 With Carlotta’s family

Mother Rosa had hoped that her daughter would follow her example of religious life. To offer her daughter to Jesus as an intimate gift of a mother, to offer the spiritual life of her “little girl” to the one Good, to have mother and daughter united in his infinite and merciful love, both consecrated to him to serve God in his Work: it was truly a great dream! The mother sought to illuminate her daughter’s future with this spiritual life. For Mother Rosa, who had known the vertigo of mystical love and had endured the severest penances in search of a path of greater love toward God and his creatures, following the one Good was a normal and desirable way of living. She said to her daughter:

“Love Jesus very much, my daughter, let him be your only thought, Jesus your beloved spouse, all yours.”74

Carlotta made friends with Caterina Rapallino, a young postulant then living in Piacenza; she confided in her and at first seemed to share her ideals.

Carlotta said: “I feel that my heart is united to Jesus.” She admired Caterina and felt very close to her, so much that she sent her this message: “You are brave, Caterina. You are truly brave: you want to be a nun and not to marry.”75 Caterina wanted to become a Daughter of St. Anne, but because of her frail health her parents refused permission. After four years she was finally accepted among the Daughters of St. Anne.

When Mother Rosa announced the news to Sr. Francesca Camisa, she referred precisely to Caterina (by now Sr. Vincenza) and to Carlotta, the two souls cared for with great predilection but still far from meeting her great expectations. This is how she expressed her thought:

“For them Jesus is on the cross all day, because they do not want to stay there or even to carry it. They leave it all on his Most Holy Shoulders; so I have thought of having it given to me, and may he give them Tabor, so that, by dint of sweets, they may become his true disciples and one day […] I may have you at my side for eternity.”76

Carlotta, however, made clear her own intentions and expectations. She greatly enjoyed the friendship of the Morazzani family, whom the good Onorata Colli had introduced to her, and their kindness filled her with joy. She discovered a more beautiful and attractive world by going to the theater (with Fr. Tornatore’s permission), taking part in family parties and learning to dance.

Her need to love and be loved, to be with people she could trust, in secure relationships, was satisfied by her great friendship with that family.

In the end the need for a positive relationship led Carlotta to meet her “wonderful prince,” Count Gaspare Barbiellini Amidei, of a noble Roman family.77 The marriage was celebrated in Genoa on 23 April 1876. It was a blessed union, fruitful in children, and Mother Rosa was certainly confident in the future of the new family.

With her son-in-law Gaspare Barbiellini Amidei

Mother Rosa welcomed her son-in-law and treated him as a son. Shortly after the wedding she wrote from America to Alessandro, expressing her feelings: “I assure you that you now have a true brother, and when you know him you will love him.”78 Mother Rosa considered that her daughter had found an excellent husband. She contributed to the spiritual good of both spouses with prayer, wise advice and every possible and necessary intervention, helping to strengthen the positive spirit of the new family.
