She wanted it to live in mutual love and respect and in the love of God. Rosa knew that Gaspare loved Carlotta and was worthy of respect and esteem; she knew that he was very honest. The cordial and sincere relationship between Rosa and Gaspare thus developed from the beginning79 and little by little became a true family affection. Nevertheless, in her letters Mother Rosa also makes more concrete remarks:

“Dear Gaspare,

if today I had not received a letter from Giuseppina and from the superior telling me you are better, it would certainly have been a bad day for me, but dear Jesus deigned to hear me, and may he be praised forever that you are better. For charity’s sake, take a little care of yourself, do not overwork, look after yourself.”80

“You cannot imagine how much your letter pleased me, confirming that you are well. I thank God for it. Why do you not all stay in the country on holiday? It seems to me too much effort, going back and forth, for Carlotta…”81

“Dear Carlotta, Nonni and Gaspare (in last place is always the most important), I wrote to you yesterday; today I write again; tomorrow I will not be able to write because I will be very busy. I would like you to tell me soon that you have received my letter in which I said I was going to Florence…”82

“Listen, Gaspare, I want you to write to your uncle, and you must do it for love of me. If it is true that you love me as a mother, you and Carlotta must write to him at once…”83

The uncle to whom Mother Rosa refers was in fact his brother Federico, a senator of the Kingdom of Italy, very influential in Rome and Genoa.

In the most delicate situations Mother Rosa always consulted her son-in-law. She wanted to protect her daughter’s health, preventing her from learning news that might upset her.

“You, dearest Gaspare, for charity’s sake I repeat: do not let Carla see the sad letters; melancholy is poison to her; and I make myself agitated by it. I will come soon…”84

Each member of the family had his or her own responsibilities. Maturity consists in giving one’s love with mutual respect and care. The son-in-law counted greatly on Mother Rosa. In critical moments, such as illnesses, her words and good advice became the most effective remedy and a strong dose of optimism.

“Listen, I am sure that poor Rosetta has had something…85 As happened to me when I fell ill again at Pistoia, and the second time was worse than the first. Let her apply the ‘Milan fly plaster’ on her chest, which will do her much good; let her drink milk, plenty of milk; the cough too is a dangerous symptom. It is better than an illness, but see that she does not travel by train, because it harms her.”

“When this ailment has passed she may do as she likes, but for now she must not overtire herself, for her health. In short, let her stay in bed or at least sitting, not get agitated, not worry; I commend her to you.”86

Carlotta held first place in the thoughts of Mother Rosa and of Gaspare. The love they both bore her led them to the utmost respect and the most intense attention toward her.

“I commend Carla to you, who is nearing her delivery […]. Do not leave her; find out who is a good midwife […]. Finally, see that everything is prepared, because it is in my head that she will deliver in a moment… Tell her to be cheerful, because three saints have told me she will have a very happy delivery…”87

Rosa and Gaspare also tried to help Carlotta in all her family tasks and duties:

“My son,

I am writing to you now; I have received your letter and Carlotta’s note, which fill me with joy. I am sending you a little package of pine nuts and sweets. I know you need toys for the baby girl; patience, one day I will send them.

I cannot send the carpet; patience, I will speak to you about it later. Dear children, you cannot imagine how busy I have been, especially in Rome, where there was so much work. So patience, because I cannot do more. I do work that not even a giant could do. Oh yes! I can do it all by the grace of God. Tomorrow Sr. Benedetta will send so many toys that you will be satisfied, perhaps even too many.”88

These letters speak for themselves: they let us glimpse the intimate thoughts and feelings of this healthy family, inspired by Christian principles, and show a hitherto unknown aspect of Mother Rosa, an exceptional woman not only as a mother but also as a mother-in-law and a grandmother. Here is an expression of her feelings in a letter to her son-in-law from Paris, on 2 June 1888:

“Dear Gaspare,

I cannot wait to come back and hope to leave on Wednesday at the latest, because I cannot go on any longer. I assure you that I feel so sad, so grieved, because the work wears me out. I am now 57, and my requests for funds and other help are endless and truly unpleasant! Oh! I would like to fly; I would like to fly even with one leg! Anyway… I hope to leave on Wednesday from this terrible… I will tell you about it later. I hope you have received my letters; take care that the children do not get sunstroke. Here there has been a very serious case of sunstroke. For charity’s sake, see that they wear a hat. I hope nothing bad happens to them! Greetings to Carlotta; tell her I will soon be with her and with you.

Farewell. Your most affectionate M. Rosa. Give the children a kiss.”89

Holiness makes one capable of the greatest and most positive gestures, because it frees the heart from every form of hypocrisy and selfishness; it arouses and sustains thoughts and feelings of goodness and altruistic attention toward others. Mother Rosa’s presence was a blessing of God that strengthened the love of her children, and she was greatly consoled to see their love for one another. To know better the people whom Mother Rosa loved, above all Gaspare, we quote a letter he wrote to his son Bernardo many months after Carlotta’s death:

“Dear Dino,

let me tell you something: I do not feel at peace, I suffer from your mother’s absence; everything saddens me; I think that now I cannot think of anything. My grandchildren behave with courage, but I do not know how my children are behaving (…); when we are alone I can speak; in front of others I do not know what to say, and it saddens me not to be able to confide in you as I did with your mother. Every room reminds me of Carlotta, and she is present at least in my imagination; she was so happy with the house, and I think her spirit would suffer if I sold it (…). Be patient and understand how much I suffer from the loss of the companion who was the center of my life.”90

Gaspare and Carlotta knew no conflicts in their marriage. They were very fortunate, because they were deeply united in love and in their children, and because of the precious presence of Mother Rosa, on whom everyone could count for advice and support.

She was a steady and reliable counselor, and not only on the human level. Her spirituality left traces and good examples that anyone could follow. Mother Rosa found solutions founded on love; relationships were important, and the members of the family cared for their everyday spiritual life, even in the midst of problems.

A pedagogy of involvement

After Carlotta’s marriage, Mother Rosa looked at marriage from a different point of view, in relation to the husband, the children and the responsibilities that follow from it:

“I wish you many blessings, I wish you a hundred years of happiness with your dear family (…); I always pray for you, I think of you and of your family.”91

She wrote this to Carlotta for her name day. To Gaspare she sent this message:

“Yesterday I had an audience with the Pope and spoke to him at length about Carlotta, Pupa and you (…). You will have news from me.”92

Mother Rosa was certainly not lazy in giving all her energies to the Work of God and in helping her own children, even though her work with the Daughters of St. Anne was very different from that for her children. Her children lived a spiritual and secular life together. She always thanked God for having taken her “from the noise of the world” and sent her to the house of the holy Mother; she thanked him for her children, called to different vocations in the world; she prayed for them and was for them a sign of God’s maternal love through significant and concrete gestures. She was always active in love and care, with her own strength and her devotion to the Lord Jesus; she carried her cross of love and of sorrow. She considered of little value, as far as good was concerned, the continual sacrifice of her own life and the daily effort to help others.

Carlotta, Gaspare and their children certainly understood the motives of her actions, as they understood their own. Mother Rosa made this clear in her letters:

“You are sad because I do not write to you, my daughter. But what can I do? If you saw all the work I have! If you saw it, you would surely say: my mother is right!”93

And again:

“Dear Carlotta,

yesterday I wrote to you and to Maria (Maria Adelaide, the first granddaughter); I am waiting for her reply; she must not be cross. Poor Mamma, everyone wants me to do everything, and I cannot: I have to go to one and visit others. I am old and must move slowly. You must be patient if I have come here (to Lercara): they sent me. And how much have I suffered? You live sheltered. I can only say that this work is little for the Lord Jesus.”94

She tried to involve them in her mission as much as she could. In 1881 she said to her son-in-law and daughter, who by then had three children:

“I have good news to give you: I have accepted a nursery school. Oh! What a lovely place, and so well ordered! If Carlotta saw it, she would like it so much: thirty-two little beds, all in a fine row. I will tell you about it later. It gives me a great deal of work, I have to do everything, but we are in a good situation (…). Imagine, we have to arrange all the equipment in via del Corso, in the warehouse. All the children must be dressed in white, in excellent quality cloth; I will tell you about it later.”95

To make the weight of her absence more bearable, she kept her family informed of her activities, as one reads in this letter:

“… I hope to leave on Saturday; I will stay overnight at Girgenti and leave again tomorrow, I will stop at Rossano, then spend two days in Naples and then I will be with you. You see, I must sign a contract at Girgenti and then another at Rossano. Do you understand, dear Carlotta? But you will be very pleased.”96

Only a holy mother could live so intensely Jesus’ commandment: “Love one another as I have loved you.” Yet her family members were not content! How are we to explain the feelings expressed in a letter written to Gaspare from Paris, a message that seems almost prophetic: “It seems that there is a contrast between us”? What did Mother Rosa’s relatives not understand, or not want to understand? In his biography of Mother Rosa, Fr. Fiocchi speaks plainly of “great expectations and material advantages regarding the financial resources of the Institute.”97 It is a question to be clarified elsewhere; here we limit ourselves to mentioning it with the primary written source that exists. Faced with her relatives’ requests, Mother Rosa was severe and firm, as her replies to her granddaughter Maria Adelaide confirm:

“Yesterday I received your letter, and in Adelaide’s you always complain of poverty. Oh! I really do not know what to say. Patience about the money. You will believe it or not, but I sent you 200 lire: check your accounts and then tell me whether I sent them or not. I do not have much money: what can I do if I have none? I cannot take money from the Institute, but I will help you in every way possible, even at the cost of suffering poverty…”98

To her other granddaughter Maria she wrote:

“I have received your message: you ask me to give you money that belongs to the Institute. I cannot do it: God himself commands us not to take what does not belong to us.

Your affectionate Grandmother, M. Rosa.”99

Living as children of God is made of truth, of gestures, of rules: they are necessary, because love must always go hand in hand with truth. To educate, to lead to spiritual maturity, to give a precise direction without compromise, is difficult and also costly. Rosa, who was and wanted to be a mother in the full sense of motherhood, knew how to seize every occasion, even one offered by a mistake, to correct the course. She was vigilant and attentive. Her love for her children had this creative dimension, nourished by the mercy of God.

With her grandchildren

At forty-six Mother Rosa had the consolation of holding in her arms her first granddaughter, Maria Adelaide, and she was overjoyed. Carlotta’s motherhood had the same roots as her mother’s. The birth of new children was a sign of God’s mercy and of his loving care for the new family. Mother Rosa looked at her grandchildren with wonder and felt them to be an intimate part of her own life. She understood the deep meaning of motherhood: a new welcome and a gift, the capacity to love with a different love, more tender and sweet, understanding and indulgent; she also felt a new desire to let herself be invigorated by these new lives, the fruit of the lives of her children.

Her relationship with her grandchildren had these fundamental qualities. To the excellent education given by their parents she added her effective spiritual and human contribution, with a positive influence that her grandchildren understood. Her wise counsels formed goodness and honesty in their hearts. Here is some testimony:

“Dear Maria Adelaide,

I hear that you work like a little woman cleaning the house; you act as a little grandmother, well done!

Your affectionate M. Rosa.”

“Dear Nini,

you will always look after Papa, you are already so thoughtful. Well done! Jesus rewards those who love their parents so much. So be careful, and do not hurt yourself in the sea sun, but enjoy yourself.

Your affectionate Grandmother Rosa.

A kiss to the little one.”100

Maria Adelaide, Carlotta’s firstborn, was her grandmother’s favorite for her good sense. A deep relationship allowed both to open themselves to understanding, welcome and a serene family life. In a letter written shortly before the feast of St. Anne in 1883, she invited her with gentle insistence to come to Piacenza:

“Dear Nonni,

I do not know how to manage without my Nonni. What are you doing, are you not coming for St. Anne? Come, you will see so many beautiful things, what a beautiful feast. Dear Nonni, come, so that we can be together. I am really worried, since you have been left alone. Detta and Giuseppina. Detta greets you and says she wants you so much.

Farewell, come. Farewell. Your affectionate N. Rosa.”101

In another letter she sent her a very cheerful greeting for her name day:

“Dear Maria Adelaide,

you are grandmother’s darling: hurrah, hurrah! I too want to touch glasses to wish happiness to all your family; I almost seem to see you from afar, all united and happy; here I hold Beppina in my arms, and she too drinks to your health. The weather is turning cool and cloudy; I also have other news, which I will tell you soon.

Your affectionate M. Rosa.”102

Mother Rosa treated Maria Adelaide with great respect. She was pleased with that girl who disappointed neither her own expectations nor her parents’; she knew that God blessed her granddaughter.

“Dear Adelaide,

I cannot wait to hear that you have done everything, and then I will take off my hat to you and call you Countess, my young mistress. Very well, dear Maria. Oh! What terrible weather this is for me! The slanders against me are falling thick and fast. Today I began a triduum for my adversaries. May Jesus give them as much happiness as the sorrow they have given me. My soul rejoices, because it gains merit; my poor body grows weak and feels ill. Greetings to all. Console me with good news, my young mistress. I remember you with love,

your affectionate grandmother Rosa.”103

Nonny too was now grown up, nineteen years old, and for Mother Rosa it was the right moment to speak to her with a certain seriousness, to reveal something of her own life, so that she might understand how the capacity to bear suffering for love of others generates a forgiveness founded on love: a forgiveness that inspires positive feelings and benefits spiritual happiness. To her granddaughter, now grown but still young, who was contemplating a future of happiness in marriage, she could offer no greater good than the certainty of the Good Lord, infinitely superior to any other lord: the love of two mothers unique in the world, a true promise of great happiness:

“Mother, mother, grace watches over you, guides you and loves you; the holy Mother and the Most Holy Virgin Mary protect you in a most special way.”104

The most special love for these two heavenly mothers was real and visible in two earthly mothers: Mamma Carlotta and Grandmother Rosa.

Mother Rosa and her little granddaughters: here is an intimate family portrait, recalling the verse of G. Giusti: “Beside the cradle, in a sweet act of love.”

“…The little girls are always here with me. I do not leave them alone until they fall asleep in the evening. Tell Carlotta to be cheerful. Nonny is well; Rosetta is ill, but not seriously. Rosetta is happy, she enjoys herself, she seems in perfect health. In any case I am here to take care of her. Let us hope that her little ailment ends soon.”105

The images and gestures speak for themselves. No commentary is needed to describe or explain the dimensions and quality of Mother Rosa Gattorno’s motherhood.

3.2 With her son Alessandro

When she wrote the story of her decision to found the Institute, many years after the events, Mother Rosa wanted to speak of the difficult decision to leave her children. She traced the outlines of a symbiotic story of her relationship with Carlotta and Alessandro:

“…as in fact happened. In both of them the hand of God was visibly seen governing them, and with special graces he kept them under his mantle. Oh, how I saw his protection materially in everything! So much so that I gave it no thought at all, thinking that God would take care of their education and their placement. […] The son, God always brought back whenever he ran away, but never allowed him to join bad company; what he did, he did because he had too good a heart, but he came back, made the holy Exercises with the friars, who gave me many compliments about him, and he knew very well how to make himself loved. I cannot express the love and respect he had for me; it was something extraordinary; he always had on his lips: ‘Mamà’; for him I was everything. […] Certainly when they imprudently told him at school that I was a nun, he went mad; the blood rushed to his head and he no longer reasoned. But I had him brought to me at once, when I was still dressed as a lay person. As soon as he saw me he wept; then he fixed his eyes on mine and said forcefully: ‘Mamà, mamà!’ How can I describe this! My heart was breaking, but I did myself such violence that he did not notice my distress at all. Shaking him, I made him see that I was not a nun but dressed as a lay person, and then he looked at those who were already in the habit and wept. All at once he flew into a rage and wanted to hit us, not knowing what he was doing. Then I thought of having him left with me (he was not yet eleven), and I won him over so gently that he made a little retreat with me and then received holy communion so well that it was a consolation. Then he went back to school and gave such beautiful signs of wanting to become a priest and made his communion almost every day. His confessor told me I had to watch over him because he tended toward penances, and he feared for his health. At that time I too took the veil, and he wept a great deal when he saw me, but made no more scenes.

I realize that I am off the subject and lost; perhaps I should not have told certain particulars which only my God knew what they cost me and how much I suffered.”106

Unfortunately Alessandro was deprived of his father, who died when he was three. He was also deprived of the intimate and lasting warmth of family life and of direct and constant contact with his mother.

Being of a good and very sensitive nature, Alessandro suffered greatly from these absences. At nine his mother put him in a boarding school in Genoa run by the Sons of Mary Immaculate, so that he might receive a good scholastic and Christian formation. In the nineteenth century it was a widespread custom among the Italian middle class to send children to boarding school. His mother, besides relatives and teachers, tried to create around him a circle of friends seriously interested in his growth: Don Accinelli, his spiritual director and longtime friend of the family; Sr. A. Francesca Camisa; Fr. Tornatore, who loved him like a son; Fr. Agostino Donadio; the good Onorata Colli; and other good friends.

Mother Rosa entrusted Alessandro to the care of Sr. Camisa:

“I commend Alessandro to you, and everything you do for him I will consider a great favor done to me. May God reward you for your kindness.”

Mother Rosa wrote this letter from Foligno in 1873. She repeated it clearly in many other letters; but she was the one responsible for her son and never delegated this task. Although far from him and busy with the many commitments required by the Work of God, she was close to him as if he were her only son. The son listened to her advice and was glad that his mother took care of him. He wrote to her:

“Poor Mamma, how good you are! But you should think of your health, which is not good. Remember that you are everything to us, not only as a mother but also as a spiritual guide. Not having had the good fortune to know my father, I have concentrated all my love on you; so I have gathered into a single parent the good I would like to receive from both.”107

Alessandro received from his mother an answer to his questions, spoken and unspoken; he received material and spiritual help and the strength of a love that revived his courage and his hope. His wishes were to succeed in his studies, to undertake a dignified career in society, and to work so as to do honor to his mother.

The relationship between mother and son, who shared so many ideals despite the diversity of their vocations, is narrated in the letters they exchanged throughout their lives.108

At boarding school

During his cultural formation (for various reasons Alessandro studied in four boarding schools),109 Mother Rosa followed his education with great interest. She was pleased with his commitment to study. His good conduct and his efforts to succeed in his studies seemed to guarantee Mother Rosa a positive outcome. But the boy found boarding-school life oppressive: the strict discipline, homesickness, the absence of his family, and psychological and physical ailments caused him much suffering. His mother was attentive to his situation and often sent him messages that reflected her love: “I feel very much the sacrifice of leaving you, but I am very glad; it is a consolation for you.”110

His mother’s letters encouraged Alessandro to live in hope:

“You and your sister should write more often.” Her visits were joyful events: “Since you are at Sampierdarena, come and spend a day with me, as you promised.”111

The boy often asked for nice presents, toys or some money. His mother always granted his wishes, directly or through relatives and friends. She was always vigilant and understood when her son was unwell physically or psychologically. As the years passed she noticed that her son’s life was changing; she understood that the negative influence of some schoolmates was having bad effects on his behavior. She intervened with wise advice and forbade him to associate with certain companions.

The son, however, was no longer docile, though he was always respectful toward his mother.

Alessandro now reasoned with his own head and made his own choices, for better or worse. He decided to abandon classical studies (in which he had never done very well) and chose to prepare for commercial studies. To do so with profit he needed tutoring in mathematics and bookkeeping.

In search of work and… of fortune

It is clear that family tradition certainly influenced Alessandro’s choice of profession. He was eighteen, did not want to be a burden to anyone, was seeking his place in the world and thought of emigrating to a distant continent, America. His mother was saddened and opposed his wish to emigrate. She wrote Alessandro a severe and precise letter, with sensible and useful advice for him:

“My dear Alessandro,

I have received your letter and, listen, you cannot imagine how much pain it caused me; I do not permit it, and it will never be that I consent. Listen, see that you are a good Christian and keep away from bad companions, and go home early. For charity’s sake, Alessandro, I urge you to leave your companions; when they tell you that I cannot support you, answer that so far you have been on no one’s back but your mother’s, and that it will always be so. I hope the job will come. Try to go to Magnini often, and you will see that by pestering him you will get it. Oh! how pleased I would be if you gave everyone a slap by enrolling in the Society of St. Vincent! You should know that I was in it for a long time, and you will see that the Lord will grant you the graces you desire. I have nothing else in the world but my God; from him I have and obtain everything;

see what graces he continues to grant me! Ah! my dear Alessandro, listen, turn to the Lord and you will have everything. I await a letter from you telling me that you have enrolled: what a consolation to see my son going to the poor to help them! The consolation would be too great for me! It depends on you.

Your affectionate Mother Rosa.”112

Mother Rosa also tried to persuade relatives to help Alessandro. Was it possible for him to find work in Genoa? Mother Rosa wrote to her most trusted friend, Sr. A. Francesca Camisa:

“Listen, if you could go to Genoa for a bit to see how Alessandro is, and at the same time go to Mr. Magnini, you know, that sick gentleman we went to see together, to see whether he has found anything yet for Alessandro; and so hear a little what Mamma says. Do you know what they have now got into their heads? To send him to America. Tell me, what do you think? What horror! Is this too what God wants? Ah! no, it is not because he is my son according to the flesh, but his soul is dearer to me than my eyes! There, in that abyss of a thousand errors, there where all unbelief is, in short the very beginning of hell for a poor young man who, inexperienced in the world, must throw himself there! Where! Alas! Do not let her notice that I have spoken to you of it, but hear what she says to you, and then you will answer what the holy Mother puts into your mind.”113

The mediation was in vain. Alessandro thought that his mother’s reasons against his plan to emigrate came from excessive pessimism. The son, who had such trust in his mother and had always obeyed her, did not abandon his plan. The young emigrant dreamed of becoming rich and esteemed, and nobly dreamed of being able to help his dear mamma. He went to Piacenza to comfort her. He explained all the good reasons for his decision and the reasons why she could forgive him. He assured her that on his adventurous journey to the unknown country, Argentina, he would always feel her presence and would always love her. He sent her this message: “Now more than ever I feel the need to love you and to console you.”114

He wrote this message from Cádiz, during the voyage. No longer able to have direct contact with her son, she felt she would be separated from him forever. She had the most pessimistic forebodings. She wrote in her memoirs:

“Today my son came to take his leave, as he was leaving for America. The pain that the thought of never seeing him again caused me gave me great grief; but far more heartrending was the thought that in those lands of such depravity he might be lost. And if, unfortunately, death should strike him, where would he go? For surely he would die without the comforts of holy Church and as a good Christian. As surely as he would forget my God, and then I would have lost him for eternity. Oh, sorrow! A creature who belongs to me will not die in the kiss of my God! Must I think that he will be a thorn in the heart of my Good? Oh, what have I done! I cannot bear so much sorrow!”115

At the height of her sorrow she invoked the Virgin, Mother of her Good, who was also her mother and the mother of her children, to help her save her son:

“How will you let him be lost, O Sorrowful Virgin? You who accepted him as a little one to keep him, will you let him be lost? Ah, my Love, the soul! What sorrow, my son’s soul! The sorrow grew, I felt myself writhing; my God, I give you everything, save his soul for me! […] Thus battered, such a great number of tribulations came upon me that I could no longer stand. Thus battered, late at night as it was, I lay down without any human comfort, alone.”116

Alone with her Good she suffered, and implored him to fulfill her motherhood: the entrance of her son’s soul into heaven.

“So, my Love, ah, for pity’s sake, clasp this son of yours to your breast, care for him and do not let him stray from your side, where one day I may see him again in your arms, saved, for eternity! Oh sorrow, which, mixed with the love of my Good, makes itself felt in such a way that I cannot describe it!”117

In the end she felt that her son, the object of so much sorrow and so many prayers, would be saved. Her Good assured her of it. We read in her memoirs:

“Then my Good came to my help: he calmed me regarding my children, he reassured me in everything […]. He assured me that my children will be saved, that he will never leave them and that in everything they will be guided. Oh, what did I not feel! A peace, a joy that never leaves me; even if I were to have the greatest sorrows, they do nothing to me. Oh, when I think of those words, that I have done the will of my God, everything becomes sweet to me and every pain a delight. Oh my Love, how can I thank you?”118

God’s plan for her life was unfolding, in the sunlit clarity of mystical gifts, as a marvelous gratuitous gift of love that involved Mother Rosa with the whole of humanity, in all the countries of the world. She no longer had a single life, but many lives to bring forth.

In the surge of love that unites, she, a little nothing, felt immersed in the power of the Spirit and repeated the “yes” of the unconditional gift of motherhood.

“What can I ever do? Nothing, for I am a nothing and less still. Only animated by your strength can I do everything. Oh my Love, how can I ever keep silent without making you known and loved by all?”119

The young Alessandro, leaving all those he loved and all his world, was not driven and moved only by the mirage of fortune and a better future. The hidden strength of his mother’s prayers sustained him in the depths of his being. He faced difficulties he had never known:

“I sleep in a hammock (inside the shop), dressed in my day clothes, with a pile of newspapers for a pillow; what do you expect, these are the living conditions in America. But do not fear, I will make my way.”120

The discomfort of sleeping in the hammock lasted three months; then Alessandro decided to rent a room. Now he confessed to his mother:

“I atone for the sorrows I have caused you by the life of privation and work that I lead. I work from seven in the morning to ten at night. But, apart from the fact that you are far from me, I am content. I eat by the work of my hands.”121

So he worked hard; he wanted to be worthy of his mother and to make her understand the advantages of his stay in Buenos Aires. On 20 February 1876 he wrote to her with this news:

“I have thought that your Sisters should come to Argentina;

I believe they would be received and accepted very well. I know the Archbishop’s vice-secretary, who is a very fine person and has great influence… I hope the next ship will bring a letter from him, or perhaps from the Archbishop himself. You should therefore be glad that I came to Argentina, because with my small help you may extend your religious Order throughout the world…”122

He considered the matter urgent and cared deeply that it be carried out. In the next letter he made these observations:

“I have spoken with the Archbishop’s secretary; meanwhile you see to it that your Sisters learn the Spanish language.”123

His mother was enthusiastic and did all she could to help Alessandro. Fortunately a letter she wrote to her son at that time has come down to us:

“My dear son,

Onorata tells me there is a sure opportunity to send you letters; I take advantage of it at once. Yes, my dear Alessandro, think that this poor Mother of yours would like an opportunity to write to you to present itself every day. I gave the 40 francs to the person you told me; think, think that I would like to hear that you are settled at last, and I am extremely sorry, because you are always up in the air, and what is more you are no longer with your cousin. Patience!

I hope you have received the linen, and the goods your uncles sent you to sell, merchandise and wine. I also saw a magnificent watch. You see that we all think of you, and it is not as you say that we forget you. No, no! Oh! my God! If you saw how many prayers this poor mother of yours says, surely you could not have a thought that disturbs you by suggesting that I do not think of you. Oh! my dear son! One day you will see whether I thought of you. You ask me about the furniture; your uncles tell me it is not advisable because it costs too much; the linen I sent you at once. I hope you will be able to do something with the merchandise your uncles sent you. Do not lose heart if something happens regarding your cousin, because you will see that money comes and goes, but the rest, which is health, can never be recovered. So take care of yourself and remember that everything on this earth ends, and only good and evil remain to us, and these two alone we take with us to eternity; the good will obtain for us eternal life and the evil, alas!

I cannot even think of it, because it would be a sorrow that would kill me. Shall I not see my dear son for eternity? No, the Madonna will keep him good for me and I shall enjoy him forever. Your sister is still in Albaro with her husband, and I assure you that you have gained a true brother; and when you see him you will be pleased. I assure you I am really in debt on all sides, but with a little economy I hope to recover and to be able to satisfy you too, sending you what you ask, but for now I am sure you will understand. Is it not so? So be patient, and I hope you will be pleased with what I have done. Farewell, dear son; Father, who is here, greets you, and I embrace you, as I am

your affectionate M. Rosa Gattorno.”124

The son appreciated the wealth of good counsel and spiritual life that his mother gave him: “How could I not listen to your advice, when every word seems to me sacrosanct?”

But in that distant country he was truly alone, and his odyssey went from bad to worse. He wrote to his mother:

“My cousin Emanuele has gone so gravely bankrupt that, if he lived in Europe, he would be in prison; he would deserve prison, but he is free and pays all his debts.”

Alessandro needed powerful friends and substantial financial means if he wanted to succeed in trade in Argentina. Conclusion of the odyssey: in December 1876 Alessandro was back in Genoa in search of work… and of fortune. Despite the financial loss, sustained by his mother’s spiritual strength and by trust in her constant love, he hoped and tried to find constructive work.

“Your letter was a great consolation to me: it is good to hear that you still love me. I await with great impatience the day when I will be employed; by accepting the job at the bank I make a sacrifice for two years, then I will certainly have a good position in society.”125

Months passed in the vain search for honest, dignified work suited to his expectations and aspirations. Alessandro patiently bore having to ask his mother continually for money. He needed a seaside cure, and Don Accinelli gave him the money required, but not enough to prolong the stay that was good for his health. He needed an overcoat and a hat; he wanted to pay the rent of a room in order to get away from his aunt Emilia, who made him live in a room without natural light; he did not want to be the target of criticism, because his grandmother and his uncle Checco “were waging war on him.” He rattled off to his mother a litany of needs and complaints, and she tried to help him. But he realized that his conduct was not good. He said to her: “If only I could be a consolation to you!”126

Alessandro always had poor health; on various occasions he had been seriously ill, even as a boarder. It is easy to imagine the pain Mother Rosa felt. She herself reveals her secret, a deep “sorrow,” in one of her moving and eloquent expressions that spring from the heart with unique urgency. We find it in a letter of September 1877 to Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega:

“Last evening the latest letter from an aunt of mine reached me, in which she told me that Alessandro is a little better, that in these days he was about to die, and I had already made a sacrifice of him to God. He is my son! The sorrow of this you cannot know; it is a mortal agony. There were moments when I felt my soul being torn from my body! Ah! what sorrow! My God, I would never have believed that in the world one could have so cruel an anguish. I am a Mother! I have abandoned them to serve God! but I am a Mother! I tell you!”

After so much turmoil, she finally felt a glimmer of hope and clarity.

The Florence adventure

The promise of a job in a Florence bank was finally fulfilled. Thanks to his mother’s friends, the young man was hired by the branch of the Banca industriale subalpina. He was received as a son of Rosa Gattorno should be received: with open heart, with esteem and with evident pleasure in doing something that pleased his mother. Alessandro spoke with humor of his two friends: “Andreotti is like the trumpet of Jehoshaphat, Mamma, oh! who instructed him? Of Monti and his wife I do not speak: you are their God.”127

Preceded by the good reputation of so great a mother, he had to behave well: moral rectitude, irreproachable conduct and an honest life were expected of him. Unfortunately he had to wait several months before receiving his salary. In the meantime he had to ask his mother for money; in every letter he asked for it, with humility, courtesy and legitimate reasons. He knew debts, problems and financial misadventures. His mother, who knew the dangers he faced, suggested that he think of marriage. The suggestion offended Alessandro’s sensitivity. Of course he thought of marriage! Why had he gone to America? He was in love with Miss Marazzani! He was still thinking of marriage! And he was certainly in love with the young Countess Rucellai. His mother took the opportunity to suggest that he ask for the young Rucellai’s hand. Alessandro, a realist, answered his mother:

“She is a countess and her family has great pretensions for her marriage. It is a serious obstacle. So there must be no talk of a possible marriage between her and me. Dear Mamma, you are deluding yourself. A rich man may aspire to marry her. I am poor and must forget her.”128

As she usually did, Mother Rosa took him from the sentimental side:

“You are a continual sorrow!”

This sorrow became a deep wound when, in a very long conversation with the director of the bank, she learned of a dishonorable fact: her son was living with a woman of ill repute and had left his job without a valid reason; he was behaving badly. He was living with one of those bad women and presenting her as his wife. Alessandro had decided to ask for a transfer to Rome.

“How one suffers! True pains of hell; it is the greatest sorrow of all that can be put together! I never felt one so acute. Oh! deaths are nothing, pains of every kind are nothing in comparison with these.”

Why had her son deceived her so shamefully? She suffered great sorrow, but the sin was her son’s and not hers. He had to be healed. It was true that he behaved immorally, but out of weakness and excessive goodness. As she had always done, she now had to help him.

Alessandro’s recovery and his “own” enterprise

Toward the end of 1879 Alessandro, with Maria Tellini, the woman he had married in the spring of that year, and with his son, was living in Alatri, in the province of Frosinone. In this small town he started a small cement and oil factory. His mother’s forgiveness had been his salvation, as a raft saves a shipwrecked man. The lessons learned from his mistakes had made him prudent, his misadventures had matured him; he was now more inclined to sensitivity, his feelings were deeper; he developed the religious sense of life. His letters to his mother in this period are like an echo of her teachings. He opened his heart to God:

“Dear Mamma, I would like to give you many consolations and to be useful in a field of work.” “But how happy I would be if I could see dear Maddalena happy; I would like to be useful to her! I hope God and Our Lady will grant me this grace.”129

His mother’s goodness had a beneficial influence on Maria as well.

“She has become very good, thanks to you. Both of us have returned to good Jesus, as good Christians. Poor Maria! She had no family who loved her, not even an affectionate father or mother.”

His mother was happy for her son; she waited with him, and now she knew that for the whole family there was a bright future of hope. His faults had been healed.

“Alessandro has really set himself right; he has taken a wife and has a son; he is so good, truly religious, and is the edification of everyone. He has set up a fine lime factory which, I hope, in a few years will need no one and will be able to give to others, because it is quite large. I hope everything from God, that he may bless it for me and make him do everything well. Pray too.”130

The son continued to give consoling news: “The factory is doing well and every day I make progress.” But he also spoke of journeys, business, worries, all the problems he faced in order to reach the position he wanted. He made many mistakes. Perhaps he lacked knowledge of commercial methods, of how to make an enterprise succeed. His dreams were not all peaceful! He asked his mother for advice as if she were a business consultant. She realized that she was somehow being used as an instrument. She confided her feelings to Sr. Benedetta Carrega:

“I enclose a letter from Alessandro, as usual! Cross, cross, you are truly beautiful! Enough; I assure you, dear Benedetta, that after seeing on all sides that it is always pretense and lies131 and that with me there is no sincerity, I have grown a callus like the monkey; nothing affects me any more, and my only comfort, you know it!”

Alessandro was sad because his mother did not answer his letters as she usually did, and also because he caused her worry:

“You are certainly angry with me because I asked your advice. But listen, dear Mamma, every time I have to make a decision I sit down at my desk and question you in your portrait. I discuss the matters concerning my business, because I believe you can hear me. So, dear Mamma, if I ask your advice in so many business matters it is because, when you tell me: ‘Do it this way,’ I feel at peace,

I am not afraid of making a mistake. Forgive me, then, if I have given you sorrow: it was not my intention. But it seems truly impossible that I should not be a cause of sorrows! I say: my Lord Jesus, I ask you to be good, and yet I always remain the same; you do not know how crushed I feel by sorrow; I fear you are ill… you cannot imagine how this thought oppresses me. But the only person I have in the world is you. My wife and my son are very dear to me, but they can never replace my mother’s love. Now the factory is doing well; I will write to you to keep you informed.”

Unfortunately the slow start of the new factory, through errors of administration, ended in a financial disaster. On 1 October 1882 Alessandro was in Rome, lodging in a rented room. Determined not to cause his mother new sorrow, he wrote to her:

“Dear Mamma, do not worry about me, everything will be settled. Think of your health, which is the only thing that worries me; the rest will be settled. So, my dear Mamma, do not grieve for me, do not think or be anxious about me: you will see, Federico will resolve all the difficulties.”132

A new intervention

His mother, in agreement with her brother Federico, found an immediate solution to the problem: Alessandro had to move to Genoa. He obeyed and did not lose heart. The courage needed to restore his business and to bear the opinions, kindly or perhaps impatient, of relatives and friends came to him from his mother, “a genius who has obtained so many positive results and has reached a high position in society.”

Comparing himself with his mother he felt so small and in need of her almost constant support; nevertheless he loved her and wished her to be happy, to have no further reason to complain of him.

“Poor Mamma, although you have so many worries for your convents and your numerous affairs, you still remember your son, and no one knows how many hours you wear yourself out with work; I, instead, at thirty, am still a burden to you and who knows for how long. But, Mamma, believe me, I do not miss an opportunity to improve my situation; but for now I feel like a child: without your help I fall. The will to work is certainly there, and soon, if nothing else happens, I will return to Genoa with more determination to succeed, to make up for lost time, and I will work.”

His new activity in Genoa was a small shop of goods in partnership with Mr. Rapetto. His mother also entrusted him with various errands: buying cloth, pasta or other goods the Sisters needed. He did everything to deserve her trust. Reflecting on the immense love his mother showed him in a thousand ways, his love and esteem for her grew ever greater: “What woman is stronger and more virtuous than my holy mother? Your son does not flatter you, because you gave him not only life, but with your virtue you helped him, and he is proud to have such a mother.”133

Despite his poor health he was engaged in many activities. But in the end he became dissatisfied with them and urgently asked himself whether to continue or take another path. He still felt drawn to America, not by the mirage of great fortune, but by the prospect of a stable and secure business.

A decision that was salvation: Gargatano

Alessandro therefore set out his plan to his mother, justifying the decision with an objective judgment of his commercial failures, which unfortunately kept repeating. He wrote to her from Genoa on 11 September 1886:

“Dear Mamma, thank you for your promptness in answering my letter. I am very sorry that you are not of my opinion, but I know that, thinking it over, you will change your mind.

Listen, I have tried many paths and have only lost money. I know I have decided to go to America. Oh! I did so after serious reflection. I know a good commercial firm that does business in America and would like to hire me as a representative. I have a friend in America who writes to me; he told me that, if I wanted to work there, I would find work with a good reference from Mr. D’Arci, who directs the railway linking Bolivia with the Pacific. There I would not have the kind of life that I almost have to lead here; so you understand that it is better for me to leave. After all, what can I do here? Nothing, except spend and lose money. In leaving I ask for nothing; I care only for my family, and I hope that you, with your generous soul, will believe that this is the right decision… So, dear Mamma, remember that I am still young and have enough time to make a good career in America.”134

This time his mother was clearer than ever in her opposition to the plan. She did not change her mind. Alessandro did not leave. His mother arranged for him to work on the Gargatano estate. And at last the son truly saw the possibility of relieving her of a burden. He collaborated with his mother in the realization of her great work, which is her glory and therefore a positive reflection on her children, proud to have a mother certainly very different from others.135

In this period he still managed to wound his mother. She learned that Carlo, presented by Alessandro as his son before his marriage to Maria Tellini, was in fact not his son. He confessed it with such repentance that his mother forgave him unconditionally. He thus had one more reason to reform his life. Commenting on the event, he wrote to his mother a few days later:

“I understand how foolish I was not to confide in you; if I had confided earlier, I would not be in this situation now. But from now on, my Mamma, you will be my confessor.”136

In the same letter he speaks of his new work tasks: he had to plow, sow, harvest, fertilize, buy a few farm animals. He also spoke of his health: he suffered from a bad cough, but nothing worrying.

The last destination

Alessandro was never in good health. He had been seriously ill several times. On 15 July 1887 his wife wrote from Gargatano to the superior, Sr. Santina:

“Alessandro’s health is not good. Since last Saturday he has had a very high fever, above 39 degrees. Dr. Albertazzi thinks it is due to a lung infection. He has lost a great deal of weight; it is pitiful to see him.”137

In other later letters the news was better. The same doctor, a short time later, assured his mother that “this is not the illness Alessandro had.”138 It was clear that the illness was there. The same illness developed fully a few years later, with great violence.

Fr. Tornatore, who was in Piacenza, was close to Alessandro in this period. He was a friend and father to him, now more than ever. He prayed to Our Lady of Sorrows and to the venerable Fr. Bernardo Maria Clausi that the son might be healed “in body and soul,” and he carried in his heart the weight of the sorrows of Alessandro and of his distant mother; he was for both a point of reference, a force of hope in accepting and living this painful reality and this extreme sorrow. He often visited Alessandro and often wrote to his mother. At the right moment he warned her to go and see her son, because he was at death’s door.

“Alessandro ardently desires to see you before he dies, because he has to tell you important matters concerning his financial interests at Gargatano. Behind these poor words I began to suspect that Alessandro wants to discuss legal matters with you; I also think his confessor has ordered him to speak to you about them. And that is why Alessandro must speak to you. I have told you my suspicion: do what God inspires you to do; for charity’s sake, if you are not well, do not set out on a journey in this severe season. Let us hope that God lets him live until you can travel.”139

Warned by a telegram from the bishop, Msgr. G. B. Scalabrini, she arrived in Piacenza on 20 January 1891 to be beside her son: a son who had given her so much sorrow and whom she loved so much. She found him unrecognizable, defeated, a skeleton, a martyr on his way to death. Every day, from seven in the morning to seven in the evening, she stayed with her son, in the house on via del Vescovado where he lived. She did not neglect the work of the Institute: she wrote letters even in the dying man’s room, and the work she could not do by day she did in the evening. The previously unknown details of Alessandro’s last two months are revealed by the letters Mother Rosa wrote. In every letter she speaks of “poor Alessandro”; she used only a few words, which describe the bare reality and reveal the feelings, fears and expectations she was living.

“Dear Emilia, what a terrible thing to see my son dying. I do not recognize him, he does not speak, he is a poor wretch. May God give strength to us, to him and to me. His resignation goes beyond what a religious could have and is a good example. Everyone is amazed by it, even the doctors. When I ask him: ‘Are you better?’ he answers: ‘May God’s will be done.’ And he is better, he eats soup.”

One day Alessandro seemed at death’s door, and he was given the holy Oil.

He asked everyone to call his mother; she came running at one in the morning. Now he could leave this life accompanied by his mother. But his hour had not yet come. He had a slight respite.

“He speaks of death as if speaking of a walk, he prays, he fears he is not patient. Oh! how edified the city is by this example! The doctors watch over him and are moved. Oh! what a miracle Our Lady has worked! The sick man suffers greatly. He is going through a true purgatory, and those who assist him suffer an even greater sadness. The pains he feels are terrible. He is a skeleton, pitiful to see. My God, have mercy! I cannot say more. The poor man suffers so much! Only the morphine injections calm him, and when he wakes he feels better. He says he wants to go away! What a bad sign! Two hours ago he called me to tell me he wanted to dress and come down. Imagine! He is a skeleton.

What a sight! May everything be done according to the will of Jesus! Poor Alessandro, he gets worse by the hour. For fifteen days he has taken no solid food, only liquids. It is terrible to see him die. The sick man also suffers from a painful leg. He weeps and says: Our Lady, my Jesus, I can bear this pain no longer. Even stones would be moved for him. He is now like a skeleton; he is so thin that the doctors do not know where to give him the injection. The doctors do not understand how he is still alive. It is a great sorrow! What can I say? So it has been decreed; we must say: God’s will be done! As for me, I know that I deserve everything!”140

Now, from one moment to the next, her son can only await eternal life. She goes over the past… relives it. She remembers so many events! One day Alessandro had written to her:

“I have my mother who loves me, who is pleased with me: what more can I desire on earth? God and Our Lady should grant me only one grace: that I go to paradise when I die, because there I will meet my father; then our dear mamma will see us there (…). I ask Our Lady to make me a saint.”141

Alessandro’s silence grew deeper. He was withdrawn into himself; his mother felt that he was losing his battle to live.

“He cannot even swallow water. It is pitiful to see him, he seems dying. Oh! what great sorrow, dear Celsa! How grave he is! He is far from everything, he never asks for anyone; since the day he received the last sacrament he is calm and cares for nothing.”142

On 16 March, the last day of Alessandro’s life, she stayed beside her son from seven in the morning. She looked at him with pity and with love. She was very sad. “How strong this sorrow is!”143

But she did not weep, because she was strong; and her son no longer saw her, and he died alone. And she could not hold him back. At five in the afternoon he entered eternal life. Now he was in the Father’s House, in the mystery of the Father’s mercy. Now he could rest. She went to her room and wept, and the Sisters heard her weeping for hours. Was it weakness? No. The mystery of death was lost in the dark universe. She touched the meaning of life; she lived the fullness of love, deeply struck by the event. But there, in the depth of God, her son was given back to her, eternally alive.

“Poor Alessandro is dead,” she writes some time later to the Princess of Fitalia. “It was a great event, awaited by the very priests who assisted him, and someone came to see me and said: Oh! how great and powerful is the mercy of God! Saint Joseph visited him and took him away during his novena.”144

Alessandro was alive; he was in the presence of God. And from this presence her motherhood acquired new dimensions of charism.

With “her” Daughters of St. Anne

The reference point of Rosa Gattorno’s choices was “the will of God.” In obedience to God’s will she had chosen marriage; in obedience she made her exodus, leaving every security behind to follow the will of Christ. She left against her parents’ requests and against the demands of her own heart. Her parents claimed the right to keep her in Genoa, the right to her filial love. But she left her family and her city, Genoa, answering a strong call to follow the will of God. She left the whole past behind her.

On 12 March 1866 she arrived in Piacenza with five companions. In that city the Work of God was to have its origin and its roots. She did not yet know “how” it would happen. She knew only, with a deep inner conviction, that the reason and purpose of the Work of God was only he: her crucified Good, whose poor servant she was, chosen by God’s “pure mercy.”

She was a servant who had to be shaped, so as not to hinder and spoil everything. She had to leave her own desires and follow him, let herself be loved and transformed, until she was totally immersed in the will of God. She walked with him and for him and fulfilled the will of God. The foundation of the Work was her death in Christ, so that she might rise.

“My Crucified subjects the humanity, gives vigor, energy and strength to the spirit which, victorious, rules over all the powers, and so well do they stay subject; self-love dissipates and vanishes, is lost […]. Pride remains conquered […]. The will, which is overbearing, my Crucified has exchanged for his own! It is sweet, infinitely pleasant, no longer to possess it. Oh! how it would have rebelled if he had not nailed it down!”145

4.1 The richness of the source

In her exodus of obedience to the Father she always sought union with Christ crucified and participation in the grace given to her: she would be a faithful disciple and bride. She conformed herself to the will of Christ.

“I was very deformed, and by his grace he made me beautiful, adorning me with his graces; he stripped me of the old man and I remained clothed as a gentle creature.”146

She became a reflection of Christ. From her person flowed an intense, inexplicable force that drew others to do good and to make consistent choices of Christian life. Mother Rosa wrote:

“Ah, my Love, what do you want? I no longer know what to give you, because everything is yours! I no longer have life, because it is yours! For, in all truth, I can say that I no longer feel alive, but in him I live.”147

This was the source of her great spiritual motherhood.

4.2 The Daughters are born in the Spirit

The first five companions left Genoa for Piacenza with Mother Rosa (three of them left the group, because they could not adapt to community life). Soon others joined the new community, which grew greatly in number.148

When Mother Rosa died, in 1900, the Sisters numbered almost 4,000. Many declared that they had decided to enter religious life among the “Daughters of St. Anne” because they were touched by the “fascinating” witness of the Mother. A glance of hers, a word, her very person had a prophetic effect: they revealed the message of God’s presence. For her way of living expressed the work that God wanted to accomplish in his creatures, those whom she loved and called to follow him closely.

An anthology of episodes of her “vocational intervention,” which continued even after her death, from the simplest to those that have the character of extraordinary events, would illuminate very interesting vocation stories. We limit ourselves to recalling the experience of two of the first Sisters, so dear to the Mother and so committed to helping her in the new Work: Sr. Francesca Camisa and Sr. Vincenza Rapallino. The encounter with the Mother, her singular call and their response are narrated in the short “Life of Francesca Camisa.”149

Francesca had come with her mother from her native town, Cortemaggiore, to visit Mother Gattorno and her own sister Luigia, who had been a Daughter of St. Anne for four months. They stayed a long time in friendly conversation and Francesca could not make up her mind to leave; she seemed held there by an unknown but very powerful force which she could not resist.

Her mother, who was already leaving the convent, invited her to leave. Francesca too was moving away from Mother Rosa’s presence when she heard these words from the Reverend Mother Gattorno: “Francesca, do you want to abandon me?” Francesca took off the veil that covered her head, gave it to her mother and said: “Mamma, I am staying in this community, because I feel that I cannot leave it.”150

The encounter, the vocational call and the response of Caterina Rapallino were different. Mother Rosa had certainly known her in Genoa, before founding the community of Piacenza. Caterina had been entrusted to her by her parents, who hoped that the climate of Piacenza would benefit their daughter’s health, since she suffered from bronchial asthma. She had already been sent to other healthy places, but without results. Caterina discovered a new mother. She felt at ease, felt herself a full member of the community, sharing in the life of that new family. She worked beside Mother Rosa, “whose presence comforts my heart so much; I feel a happiness I have never felt… a happiness I cannot describe.” She sent this message to Cento.151

Between Mother Rosa and her spiritual daughter an intimate relationship developed, founded on esteem and love. Caterina felt Jesus’ strong call to be part of the Daughters of St. Anne. But her decision was delayed by her parents’ opposition and by various other obstacles. Mother Rosa supported and encouraged her vocation. While respecting Caterina’s freedom of choice, Rosa became the voice of her conscience. On 23 December 1868 Mother Rosa wrote to Caterina:

“Caterina, you tell me that I should leave you in peace, because you always feel something calling you. Ah! my daughter, this is not me, but your spouse who, poor fellow, is dying of jealousy, because he fears that Caterina will betray him; and besides, should this voice not make itself heard?”

Mother Rosa took upon herself the weight of that weakness, like a fear of the cross. She prayed and suffered. Attached to the love of her spiritual Mother, the daughter would find the strength to say “yes.” In a letter she said to her:

“Oh! how Jesus will reward you if you know how to give him this soul. I entrust it all to you! Yes, all the merit will be yours! My dear, pray not to lose heart, if you think that I am neglectful and indifferent: a voice within me tells me that your desire will be granted.”152

But years passed before the desire of both could be fulfilled. On 9 December 1869 Mother Rosa announced to Sr. Francesca Camisa:

“At last the devil has lost a soul, and the holy Mother St. Anne, Mother of the Immaculate, has one more daughter, that is, five (that is the number of the first Sisters). One of these may be called the daughter of the miracle and of sorrows, as you wish, and this is Caterina. Now, if you write to her, she is Sister Anna Maria Vincenza.”

A relationship of “filial” motherhood

In Piacenza, in the house of the Holy Mother, the new religious Family was being born; Rosa, mother of her daughters who, having left everything to obey God’s will, were with her and, guided by her, sought only God. Rosa lived in two wonderful presences: that of Christ and that of her Daughters.

The center of the house was Jesus in the Most Blessed Sacrament. He was the magnet that drew Mother Rosa and everything in her: heart, thought and feelings drew from him meaning, light and energy. Her life was a perpetual contemplative prayer, a mystical condition, an ardent desire for a deeper presence, stronger than any other presence. It was the earthly possession of her Good, full of charity, a fruitful grain of life.

Her life was a womb for her Daughters, who like her had been called by the Father to accomplish his Work, destined to grow into an immense tree: “the work I ask of you will be great.” In that adjective, “great,” lies the only light received. Mother Rosa did not know how and when the Work would develop; it was slowly being revealed to her by the Holy Spirit, her Governor, through the events, the unforeseen and the challenges of daily life.

The Work needed secure foundations and structures. The young women who founded the new Congregation were the material needed to start the Work. Each had to be built on “the cornerstone, which is Christ,” to become a “living stone” of the harmonious unity according to God’s plan, in the dynamic power of the Spirit.

Mother Rosa received them and cared for them with an intelligent method founded on faith, a faith enlightened by the heart. She discovered their gifts and spiritual richness, the good qualities to develop, their limits, their secret sorrows. In each Sister there was the mystery of the Work to be accomplished.

In them it takes shape, and her new motherhood acquires meaning and face in the certainty of the charism.

Mother Rosa loved them with tenderness and tenacity. She felt that they belonged to her, but not in the exclusive sense of possessing them.

Above all, before being her Daughters, they were daughters of a jealous God, brides of Christ and daughters of the Holy Mother.

She guided them toward the “Center” of mutual love. She said to them: “Remember that you are God’s and therefore mine forever.”

“My God, steal this heart, that it may pour out its love, for it can never find a way to do so except in the center of your heart. St. Anne, become the guardian of that heart and shut your little Grandson Jesus inside it.”153 “Be sure that this poor Mother of yours left you bodily, but spiritually carried you away to shut you continually in the Heart of Jesus, so that in a true fusion of love you may forget this miserable one and seek only to find her and see her in the bosom of the Eternal Father… May God bless you and pour torrents of graces upon you, and may you now become a true daughter, but I want you to become a better religious.”154

“My dear, do not think that you are far from me, no, for perhaps you are closer to me than if I had you at my side. Not a minute passes that my thought is not for you and with you in your actions; in God’s presence I always try to be near you. See, my beloved daughter, think that it is good for me to settle matters here now, because when that is finished, I will have to come there and stay a good while. Come, reflect and you will see that the work of the Lord wants it so.”155

In him she embraced her:

“I can only clasp you to the Heart of Jesus, that you may soon be consumed by his divine love.”156 “I always clasp you in my Jesus and I ask him to make you grow in observance of the holy Rules and to make you a true Daughter of St. Anne, in the end a martyr of his Love. Oh! dear daughter! If you have the good fortune to obtain a drop of this Divine Love, what sweetness you will feel! Love, love, and believe me yours, held fast in the Crucified.”157

Her maternal love was significant because it was born of her charismatic vocation; it was the expression of a love given through the gift of herself to God and to her Daughters in the Spirit.

This charismatic love-gift, through her experience and personality, developed peculiar qualities of maturity, fullness and tenderness.

The Mother had already consecrated her whole being to being with the eternal Father in obedience to the Spirit, following Jesus crucified. She had done so because Jesus had revealed and communicated to her the depth and immensity of the Father’s maternal love in the position of his arms nailed to the Cross, spread wide in an attitude of welcome to all, a welcome given as a free gift: “Come to me, all of you.”

To clasp these Daughters to herself is a gift of participation in this immense love. This “ardor” of love, experienced in the intimate contemplation of her Good, was expressed in her daily relationship with the Daughters in the nuances proper to maternal love: pleasure, concern, understanding, forgiveness, constructive feelings, the tender protection of one who knows how to draw near and rejoices in the revelation of God’s love, which so well enlightens, sustains and protects his creatures.

“Blessed be God that this time I take the pen in hand to write to my daughter, to show her how pleased I am with her good conduct. Although my health and my immense occupations do not give me a minute’s rest, I still want to leave them for a moment and relieve my feelings by writing to you, because our Eternal Father teaches me that we must also give proofs of kindness to those who deserve them, just as we must scourge when there is need.”158

“I hear what you have done and I approve everything, and I am very pleased with your work; I bless God for having enlightened you so well.”159

“However, I always leave you free to do what you think; I approve everything; be at peace, my dear, I assure you that I am pleased.”160

“I hear with pleasure what you tell me about the hospital; only it saddens me to hear that you stay up late, my dear: this makes me anxious about your health. Promise me that you will not do it any more.”161

The Mother knew the weakness of her Daughters. Her loving strength revitalized them and encouraged them to develop the capacity for self-determination. She recognized in every Sister every possibility of growth and fulfillment.

Sr. Francesca Camisa did not feel capable of keeping the administrative accounts, because she was very little prepared for it. With gentle severity Mother Rosa freed her from a confused assessment of her own abilities.

“About the registers I tell you that you must do it all, and you will see that you will come out of it well: as for recording and giving the accounts, it is enough on your own, because if you pay a little attention to writing, it is more than good enough, and when you do not know something there is the dictionary.”162

Mother Rosa gave her Sisters the security they needed to overcome psychological tensions and lack of confidence; she offered herself with clarity of conscience as “water of peace.” She sent this message to Sr. Carlotta Biagini, hurt in her feelings by an imprudent and indelicate fellow Sister:

“We are not infallible, but miserable and human creatures who, if good God did not hold us up with his right hand, would sink into the abyss of our iniquities. Cheer up, for charity’s sake, do not be disturbed, because I know how much such things hurt; in short, my dear daughter, you did well to write to me at once like this; the fountain can give you water of peace.”163

She had written to the same Sister a few days earlier:

“Yesterday I received your letter; I reply at once to console you in your afflictions. My dear, take heart, because the devil is the enemy of our good works; he would like to turn us aside so that we might then yield to his desires, which are of perdition, and lead us with him to an eternity of pains. No! No! my Carlotta must be with me in Paradise for an eternity of joy and never to be parted again; always close, loving our Good Jesus.”164

With friendly closeness she encouraged a positive life and good resolutions. She raised life above pettiness, beyond “vague ideas,” toward the wonderful promise of peace that came from the source; magnanimity and patience developed and grew stronger. Her life was simple dedication, an expression of mercy acquired naturally in contact with the mystery of God. She accepted the weight of sorrows. She wrote to Sr. Virginia Gaggi on 17 February 1892 (Sr. Virginia Gaggi was then in America):

“You say that I do not sympathize with your suffering; what can I do or say? I can only ask Jesus to give me all your sufferings and to let you work in peace in the holy Institute!”

In situations of senseless sorrow, such as the grave illness and premature death of a young Sister, she wept and prayed. The deep wound received in her heart remained, and she urged the other Daughters to prevent illness, begging them to take care of their health. To Francesca Camisa, who had delicate health, she gave this advice:

“I hear that you are not well. I tell you to take care of yourself and not to tire yourself so much; and to get angry little and to eat a lot and healthily, always fatty foods. Try an egg yolk in your coffee in the morning; in short, look after yourself; health is precious. I know it now that I no longer have it.”165

To Sr. Vincenza Rapallino she sent this message:

“If you want to do me the most welcome thing in this world, you must see to taking care of yourself and staying in good health.”166

“My daughter, for charity’s sake, do not overwork; see that you take care of yourself, because in fifteen days you will be here in Rome.”167

This pressing advice was addressed to Sr. Adelaide Pezzoni, who had difficulty recovering after an illness. Four days later Mother Rosa suggested that she follow a very precise regimen.

“My daughter, I urge you not to eat salty foods, and I give you permission to say when a food does not please you. So you can ask them to make you a nourishing soup; it would also do you good to begin taking goat’s milk, or better still, if you could, donkey’s milk. Do everything very calmly… I wish you to follow all my advice.

” Mother Rosa could not accept that her Daughters chose to overwork themselves. To one Sister she sent this message:

“I am displeased with you, because you work too much and the others also work too much: you endanger your health. Could you not take a servant for certain very heavy jobs?”168

“I hear what you tell me about the hospital (in Genoa); it saddens me very much to hear that you go to bed too late, my dear: this makes me anxious about your health; promise me that you will not do it any more; leave everything.”169

A few days later (on 6 March) she insisted again with Sr. Camisa on the same point:

“I give you all the faculties, and I will approve everything you do; only one thing I cannot approve and shall always be opposed to, when you do not take every care to be well. Oh! how it consoles me when you tell me you are well. Yes, my dear, see that you do not overwork, take care of yourself and then you will be my consolation.”

There were illnesses of another kind that afflicted Mother Rosa. Trained in the spiritual discipline of “total service,” she wished to involve her Daughters in her style of decision, strength and fidelity. She loved to know that they followed “the same spiritual way.” With her extraordinary intuition she grasped clearly the smallest lack of love among her Sisters: the inclination to vanity, a certain complacency… small and insignificant defects. For her, who had experienced “the mad love of God,” they were snares, poison that could sadden and extinguish love. She was an enlightened conscience, a herald of truth; she used benevolence, kindness, respect for the feelings of others; as a mother she corrected with gentleness. She wished her Sisters to experience all the liberating love of their Mother. A letter written to Sr. Eletta Bruschi on 11 July 1873 gives a lively picture of this lovable spiritual family.

“Today, my Eletta, you will allow me to tell you a little thing about the visits that you continually receive from the young ladies of Tor de’ Specchi. I tell you this not to admonish you, but only as your Mother who is so fond of you, and who clasps you in the Heart of Jesus to have you one day near her in the glory of Heaven, where there are no more sorrows or troubles, but only joy reigns there. I would like that, when those girls come, your conversation should always be edifying, as I am sure it will be; I repeat, you must take these words as my foolish thoughts, and you must allow me, because I am a Mother, and you know that mothers always see things large with regard to their children: they will see them as saints, and yet they are never satisfied with their holiness; so here is your Mother; the reason is that everything you say will be noticed and conclusions will be drawn from it. So take care that all your words be edifying, and never answer even the slightest question that has anything worldly about it; of God alone, my Eletta, must we be concerned; the rest let us leave to the worldly. If you knew what happened to a Superior who thoughtlessly let herself fall into certain conversations about dress. My God! You can imagine what happened. But enough: I see that I am losing myself writing to you things useless to you. Let us pass, my daughter, to our little affairs: let us ask dear Jesus to keep us in his love. Yes, my God, I want my Eletta to be consumed in your side. Pray, my dear, for through prayer we have everything; it is there that everything is obtained.

Oh, inexhaustible fountain of grace; let us go, my Eletta, to draw from this fountain water of health and life. You wanted some news about the house of Death. But what do you expect? I am overwhelmed with work and cannot stop longer. Entirely yours

most affectionate M. Rosa.”

When evil enters subtly, not only is a person’s heart in danger, but it also becomes a scandal to the “little ones”; her “sorrow” becomes “the greatest.” Before a lucid conscience, sin appeared as an offense and a lack of respect toward the “Person of Jesus.” Mother Rosa was forced, against her will, to speak a language that was certainly new.

“I must speak to you in a language that is certainly new to you, because until now I always wanted to take everything upon myself, but since that is not enough for your soul, think that you must do penance for it and make amends for the many affronts made to God… Do not come tomorrow, because I am going out and do not know when I shall be home, so I think it right that it is your duty to stay and watch over those creatures whom the most merciful One wanted to assign to you. Let us not confuse our heads; let us think seriously and with judgment. It is a time of work and of much suffering in this Work of the Lord. The Church is in tribulation, and so everything that belongs to her suffers torment and pain.”170

The final, liberating blow opened universal horizons. Now the Sisters could live with greater candor. The Daughters, even when they were rebuked, understood their Mother’s strong love.

“I desire that my reproofs be understood as a mother’s love, not as punishment.”171

She was a Mother who had received a singular mission: to make the Daughters of St. Anne grow by helping them to imitate the example of the Holy Mother, the most merciful of women, an example that Mother Rosa herself imitated. She wanted to form them in the “exact observance of the Rules,” in learning the “typical virtues” that nourish the soul. She wanted them to be a holy generation; she did not deviate from this task.

“Remember often the reason why you became religious: to become saints. Therefore, if you wish, read your Rules often and try to imprint them on your heart and mind and to observe them always. God will help you to practice them, and by observing them you will become saints.”172

Mother Rosa wished every Sister to follow the inspiring principle of the Rules, which was love, a gift of the Father in Christ with the help of the Holy Spirit. It was important to her that the Sisters welcome every small observance with passionate love, as a mysterious and irresistible appeal to respond with small gestures of love to the immense love of Christ crucified.173
