“Greet Innocenza for me and tell her that I always hold her close to my Crucified, so that she may give those children the milk of holy Religion and make them true servants of the Lord and good Catholics.”281

To bring souls to God: this is the Mother’s ever-growing desire.

“It was most dear to me to hear that the Rosary is said in the hospital. My God! What consolation I felt, you certainly cannot imagine.”282

Always and everywhere the Daughter of St. Anne must remember this fundamental principle and the purpose of her vocation:

“To be holy and to be an instrument of holiness for one’s neighbor,”283

by her work, her commitment in the service of charity and her good example.

“Remember that the world is watching you and Jesus wants you to be mirrors. The example of virtue and wisdom that a religious must give is never too much.”284

In the missions

The intense participation in the paschal mystery of Christ was not for Rosa Gattorno a grace reserved to her alone, a gift to be used in the intimacy of a protected life hidden within the domestic walls of a convent; it is God’s response to the Church, which he enriches with a new Work in dispensing salvation. Rosa is convinced of it. She affirms it and often shows it in her desire and concern to see the Rules approved and the Institute recognized by the Church. She feels she must run everywhere and cry out to all. In the meaning of each of these terms lie the universal dimensions of the Church sent to all peoples. The Holy Father Pius IX had confirmed the missionary vocation of the Institute:

“They will be so many apostles who will spread throughout the whole world.”285

It was precisely in moments of obstacles, doubt and worry about the future of the Institute, when she saw the procedure for the approval of the Rules as distant and inexplicably slow, that the awareness of this vocation became clear and grew stronger in her:

“If prayer does not miraculously obtain what we seek, this sight seems very hard to me; but the right hand of our Eternal Father can in a minute overcome all obstacles, and the Daughters of St. Anne Mother of the Immaculate will enjoy the most beautiful light in all Catholicism and make it shine in all nations, and in these nations they will raise the standard of St. Anne.”286

In time Fr. Tornatore will see this great Work flourish throughout the Catholic world.287

This historic call to the missions will come later, toward the end of 1876, through the Franciscan Fr. Vincenzo Rocchi, and will become reality with the departure of the first missionaries for Bolivia. She herself narrates the event as a marvelous chronicle, writing to Sr. Guglielma Merli:

“Oh! if you had seen yesterday the fine departure of 16 Sisters, all long-standing in their vocation and so full of the spirit of sacrifice that they edified everyone. The Bishop came twice to greet them, and so did all the relatives. But with what intrepidity they answered! The Holy Father sent them his Holy Blessing; in short, they made me envious. The Superior is Sr. A. Giuseppa, the one who was named Visitor and who was at Pistoia, who has 12 and a half years of vocation, and the others too. What a fine spirit! Let us bless God!”288

With those courageous Daughters she had made a pact. Before their departure she had offered them to the Sacred Heart; through Mother Rosa their hearts and their wills were offered every day, and she made herself guarantor of their fidelity. They had gone to a distant country and left their poor Mother not to be separated, but to be ever more united in mind and heart.

On 22 January 1879 she sent this message to Sr. Giuseppa Troni:

“By now you will have reached your destination, all full of good will to edify those poor people, and you will also edify the whole city of La Paz, which watches you and your actions with a thousand eyes. I live secure and tranquil of a happy outcome, because you have solemnly promised it to Jesus.”289

She had already written earlier, while they were still traveling, to give them the joy of finding her letter on arrival:

“Just one line to tell you that I always received your letters during the journey; the last is from Spain, where you tell me that you suffered quite a bit, but were well and that you are cheerful and content and that you have very great courage. Oh! yes, this is all the work of God, that dear Jesus has communicated to you his gifts of strength and courage in the labors undertaken on so long a journey. I pray much and every morning, you will tell the dear sisters, I always offer to the Lord your sixteen hearts together with your wills, that God the Father may do with them what he thinks fit and give you strength, courage and living faith to do everything for him alone, and want nothing for earth,

for oh! how sweet it is to suffer for Jesus! How many times have I imagined being among you, but I am not worthy; my infamies hold back my step from running swiftly to the summit of the dear Mount Tabor, and I must always stay at the foot of Golgotha, to await the day of my departure to climb Calvary… Oh! sweet Love! consume my dear creatures and may I have all 16 with me in your kingdom forever for eternity… I await your letters anxiously; I assure you that I count the days, the hours, and I wrote this so that you may have my news before I have to reply to yours that you will send me from La Paz. Courage, and I am always with you; in the novena of the Child I will try to clasp him in your heart, as I am sure you will do the same for me. Farewell. May the Lord bless you and always believe me your more than affectionate M. Rosa.”290

She began a correspondence with those Daughters, using the postal means available at that time:

“This is the 7th that I write to you, twice a month, by the English steamers that leave on the 12th and the 27th of every month.”291

These are the letters of a Mother who awaits news anxiously and wishes to follow the daily journey of her distant Daughters, in a nation unknown to her and new to them. She knew that they were full of good will, of strength and courage given them by Jesus, ready to sacrifice themselves and to suffer for him, strong and faithful to the holy vocation that gives security and peace. But when the letters she punctually sent did not arrive with equal punctuality, and therefore remained unanswered, she felt all the weight of the distance and the emptiness.

“How much pain this very long silence of yours causes me: My God, what can it be, perhaps she is ill? For charity’s sake, see that you do not let any mail pass without writing to me, do you understand? How are the Sisters, have they settled well? Listen, I would not want you to act like certain ones, who, far from the eyes, are far from the heart; no, no, I do not want to believe it, because my Giuseppa cannot lessen the affection she nourishes in her heart for her poor mother, is it not so? Yes! It cannot be otherwise. Oh! I wish these days would fly and the moment would soon come when I can embrace you again.”292

With the passing of time, the lack of news is the greatest sorrow. In the doubt that the Daughters too are deprived of her word, she seeks surer ways. Thus on 3 July 1879 she writes:

“Now I am sending this letter of mine to the Consul so that he may forward it to you and so that I may have news of you, for I am in the greatest anxiety… I write and I feel really ill, I feel an agitation so great as to be unbelievable, even though my God gives me strength, and meanwhile this wretched humanity thinks up every kind of thing!”

Anguished questions prevail over the persuasive reasons that oppose a mother’s feelings.

“…Might they be ill? Might they not be able to have what they need to live? How will observance go?” Finally she confesses: “In the end it is a chaos of thoughts; take it from me with your letters. Oh! I wish the days would fly so that I might have news of you.”293

Her heart was with her Daughters, and so was her thought: “From morning to night I always think of you.” So she had promised them. It was a daily sorrow for her not to be able to visit them, advise them, help them, see their situation for herself. But she trusted her Daughters and overcame the difficulty of communication and distance by demanding to be clearly informed:

“Listen, when you write to me explain yourself a little better, because your letters are so concise that I understand little or nothing. So I urge you to write more often and in more detail. I am anxious when I see a month pass without news.”294

“Write to me often” was her repeated request. For her part she did not fail to give the Daughters news of herself and of the family:

“Since your departure I can say I have not had a minute’s rest… Now I am, as you see, visiting the hospital of Capua, where I will stay until tomorrow evening, and then to Naples, and after the visit to Naples I go to visit all those houses we have in the Abruzzi. I take the time to give you these little accounts, which will please you. Soon I will send you the Circular, which you will find to be beautiful, with many fine reports.”295 “Here we continue to have requests for houses and hospitals, and always new postulants and clothings. In a few days we have another. This year I am not calling the Superiors, because I have not yet been able to recover from last year’s expenses; I still have various debts.”296

The most beautiful news of the Family

“We have had the definitive approval of our Institute by a decree issued by the Holy Pope Leo XIII.”297

This recognition by the Church, awaited and implored, is the fulfillment, the seal of God on her Work.

“So now we are like all religious bodies and no one will be able to say anything more; only that we are true Daughters of the Apostolic and Roman Church.”298

We must respond with praise, fidelity and joy

“Now that holy Church has approved us, we are strictly obliged to observe our Rules to the letter. So, without human respect but with frankness, we say that we cannot. Courage, my daughter, for if there is no war one does not win medals and posts. Soldiers aspire to earthly posts of honor, and for us other, better posts await: those of Heaven. Oh! yes! whoever presents herself up there well supplied with medals for having fought and won, to her a crown will surely be given and a very fine place, which has nothing to do with earthly miseries. Strong as a lion and do not compromise.”299

The Mother sees in this event a sign of the Father’s blessing. Her being expands into the space of God in the generation of the new Daughters. She writes to Sr. Giuseppa:

“I wish God would send a hundred postulants, so that we might have there too a large band of Daughters of St. Anne, and the Holy Mother be loved and honored in La Paz too by a great number of Daughters.” (The Sacred Congregation of Bishops and Regulars had permitted the erection of the novitiate at La Paz. One of the norms stipulated that, six months after religious profession, the novices were to complete their formation in Italy.)300

“What a fine thing it would be if you could gather together postulants and those clothed, and, once they had done a little novitiate, bring them to me! I pray and may God grant my prayers, which are very poor.”301

“I pray”: through prayer she opens the Lord’s treasure.302 She prays without tiring:

“Oh! Daughters! Surely those who are in Italy do not cost me as many prayers as you do. Oh! no! I can truly say so!… Every day I offer you to God and clasp you in the heart of Jesus, and I pray my dear Crucified never to let you flee and always to keep you within him.”303

She prays with an attitude of essential poverty and trust and with a Mother’s boldness; from her open dialogue with God new life is born, and new gestures make life grow, develop and be celebrated. The first group of sixteen Sisters was followed by others, in 1878, 1880 and 1882. But besides sending more Sisters from Italy, the Mother opens her arms to young local vocations. She immediately asked for and obtained from the Sacred Congregation of Bishops and Regulars authorization to open the novitiate in La Paz, and awaits anxiously the entrance of the first Sisters.

“I hear that you already have a new Sister and I wish you to have many, so as to send them to me or bring them to me. Oh! I wish that time would truly come!”304

In 1882 she organizes the religious province, entrusting it to the first provincial superior, Sr. Camilla Valentini. Within a few years the communities develop, extending even to considerable distances from one another, strengthened by new Italian Sisters and by American Sisters. In 1884 the Daughters of St. Anne are in Brazil, two years later in Africa (Assab). All this requires much work. The Mother is directly involved. She understands the specific call, which defines the “second vocation of the Daughters of St. Anne.” She prepares the Sisters, sends them and, when they are far away, cultivates their fidelity, courage and gift, with the letters she writes to them. She continues to take pleasure in them and to feel herself with them.

“Well done! Forward… Work with Jesus, do everything for him.”305

“Continue always to work in these arid lands; work so that one day a fine crown may be given you. Courage!”306

“Here, then, are other Christian souls: blessed are you in such beautiful missions!”307

“You are content at Potosí! Oh well done, dear Daughter, I embrace you in my Crucified! Yes, the crown is given only to those who persevere, not to those who begin to cultivate the ground and then leave the plow and go away.”308

“Oh! blessed are you who for Jesus309

have crossed the sea and run a fine road on which to make yourselves saints, and even more, ready to bear martyrdom.”

The secret of the development of the Family of St. Anne in the mission territories is therefore to be sought in the Mother’s long entreaty with open arms, in the offering of herself, and in intimate communion with her Crucified Spouse, in total gift: “Life for life and blood for blood.” It lies in the participation of the Daughters of St. Anne in the charismatic generative force, because they too, as Daughters of St. Anne, bear fruit: “If you do well and bear good fruit, everyone will want a branch of your tree.”310

4.6.2. In the service of charity

After her husband’s death, Rosa Gattorno clearly experiences a new vocation to the service of “charity.” 1858 was for her a year of mourning, of upheaval and of… grace. It was the birth of a new way of being and of loving. We have already observed this in referring to the introduction of the memoirs. The import of the account is significant: even before expressing the feelings she experienced at the beginning of the marvelous adventure with God, she notes:

“I devoted myself with greater fervor to works of charity, visiting hospitals, the poor, the sick in their homes, helping them financially when I could and serving them in all their needs.”

God’s pedagogy develops from the reality of life, from daily events, and proceeds along the constant line of dialogue and the gift of salvation. The new relationship of love has a transforming power: “it shifts attention from oneself to others.” And these others become brothers and sisters, children of God, loved by God, to whom he himself sends us. Charity has its fundamental law, which is God’s point of view and measure: “Love one another as I have loved you.” Mother Rosa understands God’s pedagogy and keeps to the rules of the game. She lets herself be loved. She feels purified by the Blood of Christ and opens herself to the mercy of the Father. He, her dear “All,” puts into her heart his sensitivity, his impulses and the capacity to suffer in order to relieve her brothers and sisters.

“Nothing seems sweet to me on this earth, nothing! One thing only I feel: charity! Oh! what joy one feels when one can do good and help the one who has strayed to return to God! Yes, the soul rejoices in charity and takes great pleasure in seeing the good of creatures; even if the sacrifice costs much pain, it is always a consolation to see the soul relieved.”311

From the deep opening of the heart to poverty and need, compassion springs forth, the Mother’s delicate welcome of her weak creature is manifested and the festive joy of life is experienced. From death to self springs a new capacity to love: the welcome of the wounded “invalids.”

This deep feeling of mercy is a gift of the dear Eternal Father. She receives it by contemplating the Son, who took on himself all the sufferings of humanity to heal all and make them happy, and made himself Bread, Food of salvation, in the Eucharist. In him she can accept all the consequences of taking on the evil and sorrow of others. God did not ask the impossible of her, a life of senseless suffering. He gave her the joy of associating her with his redeeming work: she shared in joy in the explosive happiness of life, fruit of mercy: the return to the Father of the one who had strayed; the healing of body and spirit, the well-being, the good health of the sick. He made Mother Rosa an agent of his charity. She offers herself to the service of love.

“Make use of this miserable instrument as of your servant”

and she feels welcomed and involved:

“I will give you everything, everything you ask of me for the good of the souls who are close to you and of those you care for.”312

She understands that her charity must be inventive, must reach the depth of suffering, must enter into unity of being with the one who suffers. So her Lord did, her Crucified Good:

“He made me see how and what the charity I practiced brought about in me and how it pleased him to see me so hungry for this treasure, the taste I found in it, and never satisfied I remained… My God, how great is this Treasure in its immensity! You, O my Good, practiced it by shedding your Blood and dying on the Cross for our salvation. Oh, charity!”313

Joy, deep and intimate joy, which comes about through mystical experiences, is the fulfillment of the Savior’s promise: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.” God is love, and whoever abides in love abides in God and God in him. To live in the present. It is he who releases tender compassion in Mother Rosa’s heart. He lives in her and she lives in him. These promises are fulfilled in the mystical experience; through it Rosa loves in faith. God draws near to her, sends her to her brothers and sisters, whom he loves in his heart of flesh. Her brothers and sisters bring her to God by communicating his love to her. Therefore she exults with inexpressible joy. Even on the level of her humble daily life she sees every person close to God, and the poor and the sick irresistibly attract her heart.

The Son of God has become one of them. From the ecstasy that involves her in the fire of charity, she went to the hospitals; she speaks of it in her memoirs, where she says that she found all her happiness there. Nothing discouraged her: cleaning wounds was the most welcome thing, because it seemed to her she was doing it to her dear Jesus, and she became so involved that she had to try to tear herself away so as not to remain rapt in him.314 Therefore the cry of the poor resounds deeply within her:

“Oh! the poor who weep… what a terrible winter! I assure you it makes me sigh!”315

Mercy reaches the deepest parts of her soul in the desire to become like a miracle of love: bread for the poor:

“I would like to attract everyone’s attention to help the needy… If I could draw gold from my veins, do you know what I would do?… I would draw it from my veins until I was dry.”316

4.6.3. Her pedagogy of charity

Within this dynamism of “charity” belongs Mother Rosa’s teaching on “doing” and “how to do” works of charity. When the Daughters of St. Anne become a receptacle of charity and let God’s charity act in them, they are reborn in the newness of the Spirit; they are able to develop and bear good fruit; charity then becomes in them a source; it is an extension of the gift of motherhood:

“I hope soon to see my Daughters forgetful of themselves and all united to Jesus, with charity, patience, trust in God, courage and faith.”

Involved, penetrated by the energy of the “fire” of charity and devoted to him.

This is her desire:

“Oh, love and do not be afraid of the one you love; be afraid only of displeasing him.”317

It is important that the Daughters let themselves be loved by Jesus and love him passionately.

“Love, love Jesus and make yourselves victims of charity”318.

She advised the Daughters to develop her own feelings, the same “compassion,” the same anxiety, the same mercy, as Mary and her mother St. Anne. She urged them to be mothers in deeds, making themselves servants and a gift of life.

This mission must be carried out in the dynamism of the fire of the Holy Spirit, by strong, joyful and steady women; not losing themselves in fussiness and “vague ideas,” all things that muddle the mind and serve only to disturb us and make us irritable; on the contrary, “let us keep to the positive, and take great care to reason always with the Crucified before us.”319

The Daughters must be ready to lose their lives “with charity without limits and without reward, with a silent and hidden sacrifice.”320

Mother Rosa teaches with her life. She communicates the evangelical values she lives, and above all “charity, queen of all the virtues”; expressing her inner life to the Daughters, she becomes a teacher of charity and outlines the ideal of the Daughter of St. Anne.

On 4 February 1871 she writes to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni, then superior of the community of the motherhouse in Piacenza:

“Ah! my Eternal Father! Daughter, the heart of this God is so beautiful and so loving that there are no phrases that can express it. Daughter, do you know what blazes in this vast heart? Charity is its queen; so whoever has none of it cannot say she shares in this most blazing Love. How sweet it becomes for us when we can offer relief to the needy, how much we feel awakening in us a wholly pure affection toward those creatures, however loathsome, and if he wanted our very blood, we would soon draw it from our veins to satisfy the poor man or the sick.”

To “share in,” to participate in the Father’s charity means that he draws us out of our little programs, our little measure, and communicates to us his very strong love, a new way of being, living and acting. He loves us, and loves through us when we assist the poor. God expects us to care for the poor, the weak, children, creatures who appear insignificant in the eyes of the world. We must serve the least of our brothers and sisters, loving them in his heart, recognizing in them his mysterious and simple presence. It is a blessing to share in his creative and saving power; it is a revelation made to the “little ones,” to whom he shows his charity and the face of the Father. It is free communication in his purest love of limitless mercy.

These are the sources of the mission of the Daughters of St. Anne. Mother Rosa lives without reserve the Father’s mercy and acts as mediator for her Daughters.

She wrote to one of the Daughters, Sr. Carlotta Biagini, on 13 February 1874:

“Daughter, learn to love dear God and to give him alone all your affections: all to him, live for him, love him alone. Oh! love of my Good, when will it be that I see my daughter set on fire with your love? She consumes her life, she is ready to give all her blood for you, so give her the strength and the love to be consumed!”

As a true Mother she guarantees to God the Daughter’s fidelity, sure of the response of love: she consumes her life, she is ready to give all her blood.

United in Christ

In her courageous language Mother Rosa communicates objectively, without explicit personal references, her own mystical experience, in symbolic language.

She speaks of “fire,” of “enjoying,” of “a robe enameled with the blood of Christ,” of the “way of the Cross,” of the “Good.” Leaving aside a deeper study of her mystical itinerary, which is outside our theme, we note at once one of the symbols: blood, closely bound to the symbol par excellence, the Crucified. This symbolic word brings to light Rosa Gattorno’s mystical experience of the immense merciful love of the Father in Christ Jesus. In the Passion of Christ, in the blood shed on the Cross, Mother Rosa understands the Father’s boundless love, his mercy toward her, a poor sinner, and toward all; a love of tenderness, of mercy, of compassion, of forgiveness. A passion, that of Christ, lived in the Incarnation, carried to the extreme of self-giving, to the outpouring of his Blood on the Cross, to the last drop. It is an open book.

In the pierced heart of Jesus she is enveloped by the fire of the Spirit of love. She is enveloped by it so that she may become a gift of maternal tenderness for each Daughter and for her neighbor in the service of charity.

She shares in the mystery of her dear Crucified, sharing his passion, and leads her Daughters toward him, so that they may experience love in a living dimension.

On 20 October 1871 she wrote to Sr. Vincenza Rapallino:

“Today, Friday, I took my daughter with me into the Side of Jesus, so that there she might be consumed, made one with him, not a body to live and to feel carnal sensations, but only to become a true instrument of sanctification for our soul.

My daughter, listen to this poor mother of yours. Listen, flee often into this loving cave of our Jesus, and enter it in particular when you are sad and have some affliction:

then it is the precious moment when we are sure to find every kind of consolation there; everything is forgotten, one only tastes; no other hunger is felt than that of suffering, because the more laden with pain, the more Jesus opens to us his most loving Side… Let us take up our cross and say to the Eternal Father: My dear Father, deign to look upon me, and may this look of yours strengthen me, so that I may not only carry this dear cross on my shoulders but courageously hold it tight to my breast.”

To be with Jesus, to hide in his most loving Side, is therefore for Rosa Gattorno the fruit of Trinitarian communion, in the mystical sharing in the saving suffering of Jesus. These “extraordinary” gifts the Father gives to whom he wishes and as he wishes, and they are certainly not the measure of the holiness that accompanies them.

All her Daughters, however, are called to imitate her in the gift “without measure” to the Father in Christ and in working tirelessly in works of charity toward their neighbor. They are called to carry the cross “tight to the breast,” because the cross is life. “Without the Cross we can do nothing good.”

To carry the cross, for the Daughters of St. Anne, means to love Christ, to live in Christ, to accept as he did “every kind of suffering,” to work for him without ever considering one’s own interest, to see him in every little one, in the person who is alone, poor and abandoned.

“Let us see in these dear sick the person of our Lord, the dear Savior! What a beautiful thought indeed: that we are caring for Jesus!”

Blessed are you who can always see him with your eyes and in your heart… Jesus in the sick!”

“May Jesus be in all your works! Oh! infinite sweetness, without him nothing is good or beautiful. With him we have everything, we lack nothing, we can be certain of having him with us and we are sure of running on the right road and of doing all that he wants us to do. Let us obey and we shall be sure, sure of pleasing him and of being with him for eternity.”321

The houses of the sick, the hospitals, every place where works of “charity” are carried out, are for the Daughters of St. Anne the Calvary,322 the space of people’s salvation, in the gift of self through daily sacrifice expressed in a thousand forms, in great and small actions. All these actions are inspired and marked by the maternal tenderness poured into their hearts and by the joy of the Spirit.

The Spirit moves the Daughters of St. Anne.

To live in Jesus, to see him in one’s neighbor and to spend one’s life in order to become “victims of charity” is a gift of the Spirit.

The Spirit, the Governor, as Mother Rosa calls him, inspires her faithful Daughters with “heavenly lights”: light, warmth, ardor, strength like that of an intoxicating liquor; he grants them different qualities of being and acting.

The Spirit takes away everything that is dark, heavy, closed, hidden and sad. The Mother sees this different way of living, she experiences the transformation in faith, hope, charity, patience and courage in the lives of her Daughters: their affective sharing in the sorrows of others, their zeal for the good of their brothers and sisters and their new welcome of others’ sufferings, their inner peace, their happiness and their joy.

She wishes her Daughters to have an abundance of these gifts.

She insists on joy, as expression and fruit of charity.

“Love Jesus and you will be happy.”323

The Spirit of love pours into the hearts of her beloved Daughters: happiness, comfort, sweet honey, strength, sweetest nectar, pleasures, delights, caresses, goodness, food, drink, relief, rest.324

This language of images and symbols brings us to the heart of Mother Rosa’s mystical experience. She is given the grace to experience the richness of life in love, the fruits of charity which, as pure gift of the Spirit, are produced in the Family of the Daughters of St. Anne. She proclaims it with joy in a letter to Sr. A. Celsa Speranza:325

“Heaven rejoices at the good done by the Daughters of St. Anne, at the good work accomplished in the Lord’s vineyard, and the very Angels go about gathering the ripe fruits and bring them to the throne of God the Father. And sweet Jesus, with a look full of delight, admires the fruits of his most precious Blood.

He, the loving Lord, infinite in his love, has acquired for us so much wealth, to be used to raise our poor souls to the heights of eternal life, which are gained only with toil and suffering. Love… love!”

In the family style: compassionate love, faith and hope.

In her instructions on the practice of charity the Mother, besides her personal experience, draws on the Rule of 1869, interpreting it with creative vision and living freedom. The Rule, chapter 8, paragraph 1, says:

“My daughter… my Heart was a sea of compassion for the spiritual and bodily miseries of my neighbors. In this I was a perfect portrait of Jesus Christ, to whom the dearest work, and the one most recommended to his followers, was the care of the sick.

To draw us to this exercise of charity, the most repugnant to fallen nature, he assures us that the care given to the sick he regards as given to himself.

You, my daughter, are called to imitate me in this compassionate charity.”

Mother Rosa observes:

“All the Daughters must keep before them the Divine Model Jesus to correct their way of thinking and acting, especially with regard to that charity which I so much recommend, and in which our Mother St. Anne was so great.”326

“Take comfort, you who labor for your Jesus, because in touching the sick with charity (and that great charity which our dear Mother St. Anne had), in touching those infirm creatures, you touch Jesus who is found in them. Ah! what a thought, my Daughters!”327

“Knowing that, when you stand before the sick person, you stand before Jesus, you will conduct yourself with humility and modesty, you will speak in a low voice, you will speak of things that at once relieve the sick person and edify those present.”328

Mother Rosa used to say:

“I recommend to you the care of the sick: go to them with love and respect, as if you were going to visit Jesus; if you happen to fall asleep, try to wake up and do everything possible to stay awake (the nursing Sisters also took night shifts).

I must think that I am in the presence of Jesus and that he will take account of everything I do for the sick.

You see, I went to care for the sick for 25 years, and it seemed to me that I was going to Paradise. You see, this is the only consolation we can have on this earth; I have not felt it again since I gave up this work.

Yes, you must do everything in a spirit of faith. I am in this hospital, I tend this woman whose body is full of worms, I relieve her suffering. Ah! what delight, when I think I am relieving a person who belongs to Jesus; there is no other work that gives such consolation: to go home in the morning and say: I have dressed the wound of my Jesus! You will tell me: but I have not felt these delights; ah! it means that you have not done this work in a spirit of faith! Why do we let so much toil go to waste? Why do we act like so many servants? Ah yes, the Lord has always had a predilection for nurses!”329

“My daughter, among the works of my Institute, the care of the sick is the noblest and the most meritorious. By this work you, my daughter, imitate that compassionate charity of my heart toward the sufferings of men; this work made me very like my Immaculate Daughter and my Grandson Jesus… Here, then, my daughter, is the gain you must remember when you think of your care of the sick: you, as my daughter, bring with you my compassionate charity toward your brothers and sisters, that charity which will kindle in your heart a flame, which will inflame you with the desire to please God and to glorify him in eternal salvation, the salvation of the souls and bodies of your brothers and sisters; and therefore you will feel great pain, sadness and sorrow in seeing them far away and in danger of losing the eternal salvation of the soul, a pain and anguish that in the end will make you die sad and crucified with Christ Jesus.”330

From these principles Mother Rosa draws norms of practical conduct in her conferences to the nurses:

“For charity’s sake, do not abandon the sick to go to Mass; if you do, how can you receive communion after abandoning Jesus in his illness, who needed your help? What will you tell him? What will he tell you?

You abandoned me while I suffered and now you come to receive me? If this happens on a feast day, tell the superior, who will send two other Sisters and will notify me. Mass is celebrated also later in the day, and then you will be able to say to Jesus: Jesus, I suffered for you all night, I brought you a soul, and now I come to receive my reward, to receive you in my soul.”

And she continues:

“There are men who want nothing to do with religion. Do not speak to them of it; many times it is better to leave them alone. Let them be distracted, and you will see that little by little they will return to religion and will do what you ask of them.”331

The Daughters of St. Anne will always try to see how much light there is in people’s hearts, because they know that God is the merciful Father who always awaits the return of his children. In serving the bodily needs of the sick, they will practice the service of light for souls, so that the flame of faith may shine and their brothers and sisters may enjoy salvation.

“My daughter, you must know how to unite the care of the sick with the exercises of piety established in the holy Rules. From these holy exercises you will receive that enlightened faith which will make you understand that, in caring for the sick, you serve Jesus; that firm hope which, through the wearing out of your strength and your body, will give you a foretaste of the delightful and eternal life that will be given you as a reward for the loss of the present life; that charity which, in serving the sick, seeks only the pleasure your God takes in having you as companion in relieving the body of the sick person in his ills, but with that intention, the same with which God relieves suffering, that is, the intention of healing his soul of the sickness of sin, if it is struck by it, and of uniting it to God.”332

So that the Daughters might not turn away from that sublime mission, Mother Rosa prays without ceasing:

“I always offer to the Lord your hearts, Daughters, your will, that God the Father may do with them what he thinks fit, and give you strength, courage and living faith to do everything for him alone and nothing, nothing for earth.”333

Hope gives wings to desire and to the sense of life:

“Daughters of St. Anne, my beloved, courage, for one day you will see your God and enjoy your labors; and the more one has procured, the greater will be her beatitude.”334

The maternal style in service.

The Rule of 1869 marks with decision and emphasis the fundamental attitude of the Daughters of St. Anne in the work of charity.

“You must consider yourself as the mother.”

It is a compendium; one might say a symphony of the feelings and personal spiritual richness proper to a person in her being a WOMAN. It means gratuitousness, attention, humility, meekness, patience; to be a mother, for the Daughter of St. Anne, means compassion (suffering with others), effective service that overcomes evil and seeks good.

Mother Rosa said to the Daughters:

“You must consider yourself as the mother of the poor sick; you will love them with a maternal love; you will pray for them, and you will weep over their spiritual and temporal ills.”335

The Mother recommended to the Daughters:

“Help one another and often remember to imitate the charity of your Mother St. Anne. True charity toward the neighbor. To love those who suffer, to suffer with them.”336

“Treat your neighbor with gentleness and love.”337

“Daughter, be good to everyone and set a good example to the dear sick.”338

“Oh, I would like to see you… in the sweet wards, close to the bed of Jesus, now dressing his wounds, now doing for him what he needs!… and so he may give your heart those sweet throbs of love; every morning I tell him to consume you in it.”339

Mother Rosa is the Mother of the Daughters whom “God has entrusted to her.”340

“You will not tire of procuring for them every bodily and spiritual relief… every innocent consolation; so that in this way they may see in you a Mother who, forgetful of herself, thinks only of making them happy.”341

“I hold the (educators) close to my Crucified, so that they may give the children entrusted to them the milk of holy Religion, that they may grow up true servants of the Lord and good Catholics.”342

“Let the teachers strive to draw the hearts of the girls to themselves so as to make them docile, good and dear to the Lord, and let them begin to live in the Lord. How sad the thought of how many hearts I could have given to Jesus, and instead how many, through my fault, have been lost!”343

The maternal style with which Mother Rosa forms her Daughters is not a marginal aspect of her charism.

It is the central value of her charism, in the sense that it expresses, through a style of life and positive works, the merciful love of the Father, revealed in the evangelical ideal of clarity expressed by Jesus: to love without seeking return, to give even one’s life if need be without expecting reward, to lose so that others may grow. So does the Father in Christ. To act in unity of love to please the Father and in close union with the Crucified is at the summit of Mother Rosa’s desires, it is her response:

“Ah! dear Good, I have given to eat, I have distributed your word, in short everything on the wings of Providence!”344

In the Family of the Holy Mother of Mary Immaculate there can be no other point of view, no other style, no other law than the maternal gift of the service of life. She had already put into practice this new, creative and different way of living in the Motherhouse from the origins of the Institute:

“Meanwhile we give them to eat (she speaks of the poor and abandoned girls), we take them out of sin, we teach them to love God! The Eternal Father will take care of the rest. What do we have here, my dear?”345

Who gave us the income to pass the soup to these hungry girls? God! Yes, my dear, prudence yes, but not a prudence like that of today, whereby to do a little charity we religious must be paid at the top of the house.

What horror, ugly spirit! Our holy (Rule), which is full of charity, does not please us, it abhors it.

Courage, forward, here I accept postulants with all my might.”346

The Daughters must welcome this specific quality of being and acting, if they want to live according to the particular gift of their religious Family, which qualifies their “following” of Christ: to reveal the maternal face of God, to be sign and instrument of the Father’s mercy, of the intimacy of a love that “touches” them, that is deeply moved by the poverty of his children, by the suffering they live, by their cry of pain, by the sadness of their abandonment.

A love close to Christ becomes strong in the power of his Cross; the Daughters share, in their inner thoughts and feelings, in the life of Jesus, in his passion for the human being, and are involved in a fruitful mission of salvation.

They carry out this mission with the utmost fidelity to Mother Rosa’s founding charism. In this fidelity lies the special strength of the Family of the Daughters of St. Anne.

In the biographical and spiritual itinerary of Mother Rosa, seen under the charismatic aspect of her maternal mission, two culminating moments appear evident:

The first moment culminates in her human motherhood (the years from 1853 to 1857, the birth of her three children).

Her remote upbringing, from childhood to the end of adolescence, and her more specific preparation for marriage and married life contributed to it.

The second moment is centered on her spiritual motherhood (from 1866, the foundation of the Institute, until her death in 1900).

It is the epilogue of an experience of extreme sorrow, the trauma of the death of her husband and of her youngest son, and of a profound encounter with God.

She discovers her vocation in the Church, in the gift of self to share in the mission of salvation, through the “propagation of the faith” and the service of charity to the poor and the sick.

In her relationship with God, her faith followed an evolutionary line of development that began when she was still married.

For her God was fundamentally the provident Lord, who loves his children, cares for them, guides them toward the good, and manifests his will through the “commandments.”

She is sure of this faith and leads her life aiming to reach the center of God’s will, and lets herself be guided in this direction also by the mediation of those who represent him.

In this “structural” core of faith she lives the joys of motherhood.

Inspired by the intimate experiences of life, she is enriched by them. Her feminine being expands in being a mother. She shares in the vital energy of the Creator. But having reached this culminating moment, the path does not follow the plan she had traced.

A sudden change interrupted the normal development she had reasonably planned and awaited. Her family plan, intelligently conceived and carried out, collapsed.

At this point God entered her family history, so that it might become once more a place of encounter with his will to save all people.

This fact places Mother Rosa Gattorno directly in God’s school, so that she may let herself be guided by him each day in the unpredictable events of her life.

For her God becomes more important than every evidence; he is no longer only the God of obedience, he is the God of LOVE, who gives his only-begotten Son for the salvation of mankind.

Mother Rosa opens her soul to his power. And when, through the mediation of Pope Pius IX, God asks her for the sacrifice of her children, she, like Abraham, definitively adheres to his design.

“I feel strong as a giant.” Her faith thus reaches the peak of unconditional obedience.

In the Church she founds a new Family, the Daughters “of the promise.” With the new mission she receives a new name: MOTHER.

(In the religious Family of the Daughters of St. Anne the present custom is to call “Mother” only the Superior General, as representative of Mother Rosa.)

From the numerous Daughters she formed emerges the culmination of divine mercy, which reaches Mother Rosa through the blessed Womb of Mary, closely united to her Mother St. Anne; the face, character and heart of the Family are formed in the Work, which extends the Family of the Mother of Mary Immaculate in the plan of salvation.

For God’s Work Mother Rosa gives her whole life, to the extreme limit.

Concrete facts prove it, and they are so well known that they need no support from testimonies or other forms of confirmation.

Suffice it to cite one alone which, by the authority of the witness, Fr. G. B. Tornatore, who was very close to her as co-founder of the Family, and by the terms in which he expresses himself, seems a synthesis of all the others: “What a woman! How she sacrifices herself for the Institute! Oh, she is a creature truly faithful to her God. She lives only to do the Work that God has chosen for her.”347

This dedication is part of her maternal being. She gives her motherhood to the Church, to the poor, to girls in difficulty, to the sick, to all who need her love, with an immediate response.

It is a gift of motherhood first of all for the Daughters, whom she involves in the new kind of presence and service in the Church.

The Daughters, called by her to the Father’s Work, discovered in it what the Spirit had already inspired in them. They saw themselves reflected in her attitudes, expressed their own desires in her, listened to her and followed her.

From this convergence of ideals and aspirations the Family of the Holy Mother of Mary Immaculate is born and develops, with remarkable growth and success.

The Mother welcomes each Daughter as a tender plant to be cultivated; she cares for her, strengthens her, with that very human, maternal love, “which is a great hidden force, a warmth that is poured upon the seed.”348

It is a warmth that brings about in each Daughter, and in the whole Family, the action of the Spirit.

She is wholly for the good of the Daughters and for the consolidation of the Work, with a combative energy, without pause and without measure.

“My dear, I can assure you that this wretched woman, everything she has done and said, her thought was always for your good, and a thousand times I neglected myself for your good.”349

Mother Rosa recognizes the spiritual richness with which the Daughters take part in God’s Work, and delights in it. In her deep humility she feels she receives so much from them. She thanks them. Only God can reward, and she asks it of him:

“My blessed creatures, believe that this poor Mother of yours will be grateful to you for eternity. If on this earth she prays for her daughters, for their spiritual and temporal good, so as to leave them well supported and firmly grounded in virtue and in means, in Heaven, if I go there by the mercy of God the Father, be sure that my prayers will be such that, if they are granted, you will surely be happy.”350

At the end of her earthly life, on 6 May 1900, she had very many Daughters to pray for: almost 4,000.

Her maternal mission did not end with the end of her great life. In the “eternal enjoyment,” the greatest aspiration of her life, she contemplates the mystery of her God: the Eternal Father, Christ her Good, the overwhelming Spirit of love.

She lives in the fullness of life, she lives in the today, just as she defined herself: “your Mother for all eternity.” She is the womb of new spiritual lives. Her numerous Daughters who follow her feel themselves won over by the Spirit, by her charism, by her vital energy that penetrates reality in the dimensions of space and time, of breadth and length.

Present with God, she is also present, in a mysterious way, in the Family of the Daughters of St. Anne, in her Family, with the witness of her life and with her very timely teaching; a teaching well suited to the needs of today, contained in her writings, above all in her correspondence, which the present research has frequently consulted. Through these sources one can discover Mother Rosa’s intimate spiritual world. One can discover the intimacy of her world;351 one can come to know “the great works accomplished by her, by the power of the Good and of the Holy Mother.”

To rediscover her in the vital and strong relationship of motherhood, to let oneself be nourished by the Mother’s ideas, means for every Daughter of St. Anne to welcome the dynamic force of the “charism” and to live according to her teachings in the historical present that runs swiftly toward the twenty-first century.

To make it living and relevant in an intelligent form of maternal dedication, inventive and inexhaustible, expressing and bearing witness to the motherhood of God, who wishes to express himself in a love of merciful tenderness toward every man and woman of our distant and restless world.

It means above all to see God “near” us, walking with us, today as yesterday.

We must let ourselves be kept by God, let ourselves be welcomed by God, and be freed from fear, which is felt more today than yesterday; we must free ourselves from the alienating conditioning of “mass culture”; we must listen to the story of Mother Rosa and our own story in the TRUTH and in the luminous clarity of his WORD, the only Word that gives “meaning” to life, to our origins and to our destiny.

It means welcoming the Father’s plan, walking in his way with courage and fidelity, looking to the future, toward the luminous Mount of freedom: Calvary.

It means being and going always with him, in him and for him.

Mother Rosa explains it to us with her overwhelming strength, with her very timely witness:

“…Forward: the earth is large, the field is immense. Enter, and never turn back; always think of what you have not done, not of what you have already done. It is a mistake to believe you have already done something.”352
